title: Rare Disease Classification in Video Capsule Endoscopy
summary: Video capsule endoscopy offers a non-invasive way to examine the small bowel, however, the rare but clinically important findings that appear only in less than 1\% of labelled frames, provide very less signal for detection. As a result, while models can achieve high overall performance, they almost completely miss these rare findings. We condition each frame's decision on evidence from the rest of that patient's video, not on the frame's own posterior alone, supplying information a single frozen frame can never contain. Building upon Expected Gain Arbitration, a per-frame, macro-F1-optimal correction over the confusion matrix, we further compose it with video-disease-presence conditional resulting in our decoding method Hierarchical Conditional-Expected-gain (HCE). We evaluate HCE on two independent VCE datasets, Kvasir-Capsule and GALAR, against a static temporal-smoothing baseline and an optimal-transport (OT) frame-level correction. HCE significantly improves rare-class recall over a temporal-smoothing baseline on GALAR (2.7--3.1x; 95\% CI excludes zero in both scopes) and shows a similar, though not statistically confirmed, gain on Kvasir-Capsule (up to 3.4x). Against OT, HCE still improves rare-class recall in all four evaluation settings (+0.016 to +0.029), and additionally improves macro-F1 and MCC.

AI.tldr: HCE, a hierarchical decoding method combining video-level disease presence with per-frame Expected Gain Arbitration, boosts rare-class recall in video capsule endoscopy without per-frame posterior reliance.
AI.motivation: Rare but clinically important findings appear in <1% of labeled VCE frames, giving weak signal; models achieve high overall performance but almost entirely miss these rare findings.
AI.method: Condition each frame's decision on evidence from the rest of the patient's video. Build on Expected Gain Arbitration (per-frame, macro-F1-optimal correction over the confusion matrix), composed with video-disease-presence conditioning to form Hierarchical Conditional-Expected-gain (HCE).
AI.result: Evaluated on Kvasir-Capsule and GALAR. HCE significantly improves rare-class recall vs temporal-smoothing on GALAR (2.7-3.1x, 95% CI excludes zero) and similar non-confirmed gain on Kvasir-Capsule (up to 3.4x). vs OT, HCE improves rare-class recall in all four settings (+0.016 to +0.029), plus macro-F1 and MCC.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging patient-level video context enables a decoding method that substantially recovers rare-class detection in VCE, outperforming temporal smoothing and optimal-transport correction baselines.

title: Brain scaling and diversity in musteloids
summary: The diversity of brain size and organization across mammals reflects how evolutionary and ecological pressures have shaped neural architecture through time. Yet, how these selective pressures translated into measurable variation in the proportions and overall shape of the brain across species remains poorly understood. In this study, we used high-resolution virtual endocasts from 41 musteloid species (e.g. otters, skunks, raccoons) to quantify variation in endocranial composition and shape. We analyzed both the complete endocast and its principal subdivisions (olfactory bulbs, cerebrum, and hindbrain) using a combination of compositional data analysis and 3D geometric morphometrics. Phylogenetically informed regressions (PGLS) and model comparisons were used to assess the effects of endocranial size, locomotion, diet, and taxonomy on both the regional proportions and the overall shape of the endocranial cast. Musteloid brain organization is mostly driven by size-dependent scaling: larger brains have enlarged cerebra, reduced olfactory and hindbrain regions, and rounder endocasts. However, some lineages markedly deviate from this largely conserved allometry: otters (Lutrinae) exhibit proportionally enlarged cerebra and strongly reduced olfactory bulbs, whereas skunks (Mephitidae) show the reverse pattern, emphasizing enhanced olfactory investment. Feeding ecology also contributes to variation in brain organization, as piscivores show disproportionately smaller olfactory bulbs compared with other feeding guilds. In contrast, locomotor mode has little explanatory power for either endocranial composition or shape. Brain evolution in musteloids is therefore not uniform: a common scaling pattern dominates, but lineage-and diet-specific adjustments modify how brain regions are proportioned.

AI.tldr: Using high-resolution virtual endocasts from 41 musteloid species, this study shows brain organization is mostly driven by size-dependent allometry, with lineage- and diet-specific deviations (otters, skunks, piscivores).
AI.motivation: The diversity of mammalian brain size and organization reflects evolutionary and ecological pressures, but how these pressures translate into measurable variation in brain proportions and shape across species remains poorly understood.
AI.method: High-resolution virtual endocasts from 41 musteloid species were used to quantify endocranial composition and shape. The complete endocast and principal subdivisions (olfactory bulbs, cerebrum, hindbrain) were analyzed using compositional data analysis and 3D geometric morphometrics. Phylogenetically informed regressions (PGLS) and model comparisons assessed effects of endocranial size, locomotion, diet, and taxonomy on regional proportions and overall shape.
AI.result: Brain organization is mostly driven by size-dependent scaling: larger brains have enlarged cerebra, reduced olfactory and hindbrain regions, and rounder endocasts. Otters (Lutrinae) show enlarged cerebra and reduced olfactory bulbs; skunks (Mephitidae) show the reverse with enhanced olfactory investment. Piscivores have disproportionately smaller olfactory bulbs. Locomotor mode explains little variation in composition or shape.
AI.conclusion: Musteloid brain evolution is not uniform: a common scaling pattern dominates, but lineage- and diet-specific adjustments modify how brain regions are proportioned.

title: Nonequivalence of expected free energy and revised system integrated information in noisy permutation networks
summary: The free-energy principle (FEP) and active inference describe adaptive systems through probabilistic generative models and free-energy functionals, whereas integrated information theory (IIT) characterizes intrinsic cause-effect organization. We separate two questions: whether revised IIT quantities admit local free-energy-like representations and whether scalar expected free energy can determine system integrated information. We show that the 2026 IIT intrinsic-differentiation and specification terms admit exact surprisal representations, and hence variational-free-energy representations under exact inference. We then construct noisy binary permutation networks whose causal topology varies while local transition reliability is fixed. In a homogeneous state, all permutations yield the same one-step predictive distribution and state-risk expected free energy under common preferences and observation models, yet revised IIT distinguishes them: multicycle permutations have zero whole-system integration, whereas a single noisy cycle has positive integration at intermediate reliability. For an n-unit noisy single cycle, we derive a closed-form expression for revised system integrated information, prove that the minimum-information partition cuts exactly two causal edges, and show that as n grows the optimal reliability approaches unity, the joint specified-state probability approaches one half, and the maximum integration approaches one ibit. Numerical IIT calculations for n = 2-5 and exhaustive partition enumeration through n = 8 reproduce the analytical results. Thus, local surprisal/free-energy correspondence coexists with global non-equivalence: equal expected free energy does not imply equal revised IIT system integrated information. Any synthesis of IIT with FEP/active inference must retain counterfactual causal information beyond a scalar free-energy value.

AI.tldr: Revised IIT quantities admit local surprisal/free-energy representations, but scalar expected free energy cannot determine system integrated information; equal EFE does not imply equal IIT integration.
AI.motivation: To clarify the relationship between the free-energy principle/active inference (probabilistic generative models, free-energy functionals) and integrated information theory (intrinsic cause-effect organization) by separating two questions: whether revised IIT quantities admit local free-energy-like representations, and whether scalar expected free energy can determine system integrated information.
AI.method: Shows 2026 IIT intrinsic-differentiation and specification terms admit exact surprisal (hence variational free-energy) representations under exact inference. Constructs noisy binary permutation networks with varying causal topology but fixed local transition reliability. Analyzes a homogeneous state where all permutations share one-step predictive distribution and state-risk expected free energy. Derives closed-form revised system integrated information for an n-unit noisy single cycle, proves the minimum-information partition cuts exactly two causal edges, and validates with numerical IIT calculations (n=2-5) and exhaustive partition enumeration (n=8).
AI.result: All permutations yield identical one-step predictive distribution and state-risk EFE, yet revised IIT distinguishes them: multicycle permutations have zero whole-system integration, while a single noisy cycle has positive integration at intermediate reliability. For the n-unit cycle, minimum-information partition cuts exactly two edges; as n grows the optimal reliability approaches unity, joint specified-state probability approaches 1/2, and maximum integration approaches one ibit. Numerics reproduce analytical results.
AI.conclusion: Local surprisal/free-energy correspondence coexists with global non-equivalence: equal expected free energy does not imply equal revised IIT system integrated information. Any synthesis of IIT with FEP/active inference must retain counterfactual causal information beyond a scalar free-energy value.

title: GCTAg: scalable mixed-model analysis for biobank-scale agricultural cohorts
summary: Genome-wide association studies identify genomic variants associated with traits. Mixed linear model association (MLMA) methods using a whole-genome relationship matrix, such as those implemented in GCTA, are powerful but computationally expensive. Here, we remove key memory and CPU bottlenecks in GCTA, reducing REML memory usage by nearly 75% and substantially accelerating MLMA by orders of magnitude in biobank-scale cohorts while preserving exactness. We further exploit relatedness in the mapping cohort through a reduced-rank Woodbury matrix approach, delivering further orders of magnitude performance gains with controlled genomic inflation. Native on-the-fly dominance recoding also eliminates slow I/O-operations on intermediate files, enabling efficient additive and dominance MLMA analyses in large agricultural cohorts.

AI.tldr: This paper removes memory and CPU bottlenecks in GCTA's mixed linear model association (MLMA), achieving up to 75% REML memory reduction and orders-of-magnitude speedups at biobank scale while preserving exactness.
AI.motivation: GCTA-style MLMA methods using a whole-genome relationship matrix are powerful but computationally expensive, especially in terms of memory and CPU at biobank scale.
AI.method: Optimizes GCTA to remove key memory and CPU bottlenecks; exploits relatedness via a reduced-rank Woodbury matrix approach; introduces native on-the-fly dominance recoding to avoid intermediate-file I/O.
AI.result: REML memory usage reduced by nearly 75%; MLMA substantially accelerated by orders of magnitude in biobank-scale cohorts while preserving exactness; further orders-of-magnitude gains with controlled genomic inflation; efficient additive and dominance MLMA in large agricultural cohorts.
AI.conclusion: The proposed optimizations make exact MLMA practical and scalable for biobank-scale and large agricultural cohorts, including dominance analyses.

title: MathAgent: Multi-Agent Optimization of Mathematical Invariants for Molecular Property Prediction
summary: Mathematical invariants provide complementary representations of molecular structure, but their predictive utility can vary across datasets and prediction tasks. For a new dataset, appropriate construction of invariant representations from algebraic topology, differential geometry, topological spectral theory, and commutative algebra is a challenging task, particularly when evaluating multiple representations is computationally expensive. We develop a Mathematical Agentic Model (MathAgent) to automatically optimize invariant representations in molecular property prediction. The framework combines dataset-aware representation design, low-cost candidate screening, and progressive evaluation. Language-model reasoning supports task interpretation, strategy proposal, and workflow coordination, while scientific computations and numerical decisions are carried out by deterministic tools. We evaluate MathAgent on protein--ligand binding-affinity and quantitative toxicity prediction tasks. Different datasets favor different combinations of mathematical invariants, demonstrating the need for dataset-adaptive representation selection rather than a fixed universal representation. Objective-conditioned executions further show that the framework can adjust its evaluation strategy according to user-specified goals. MathAgent therefore provides a systematic, evidence-driven, and traceable approach for optimizing mathematical invariant representations and reducing reliance on manual configuration and/or experimentation in molecular property prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MathAgent, a Mathematical Agentic Model that automatically optimizes mathematical invariant representations for molecular property prediction via dataset-aware design, low-cost screening, and progressive evaluation.
AI.motivation: Mathematical invariants offer complementary representations of molecular structure, but their predictive utility varies across datasets and tasks. Choosing appropriate invariant representations from algebraic topology, differential geometry, topological spectral theory, and commutative algebra is difficult, especially when evaluating multiple representations is computationally expensive.
AI.method: MathAgent combines dataset-aware representation design, low-cost candidate screening, and progressive evaluation. Language-model reasoning handles task interpretation, strategy proposal, and workflow coordination, while deterministic tools perform scientific computations and numerical decisions.
AI.result: Evaluated on protein–ligand binding-affinity and quantitative toxicity prediction, different datasets favored different combinations of mathematical invariants. Objective-conditioned executions showed the framework can adjust its evaluation strategy to user-specified goals.
AI.conclusion: MathAgent provides a systematic, evidence-driven, and traceable way to optimize mathematical invariant representations, reducing reliance on manual configuration and experimentation in molecular property prediction.

title: Stability of Phase-locked States of Weakly Coupled Izhikevich Neurons
summary: The Izhikevich model is a computationally efficient neuron model that can exhibit a wide range of firing patterns observed in the brain. However, it is a discontinuous dynamical system, which means the methods for applying weakly coupled oscillator theory developed for continuous dynamical systems cannot be applied. Therefore, the collective behaviour of coupled Izhikevich model has not been fully studied. To our knowledge, we carry out the first computation of the phase model for an Izhikevich neuronal model with chemical synapses. Using the phase model we study the existence and stability of phase-locking states and how these vary with parameters. Moreover, we find an interesting connection between the stability of anti-phase states of the phase model and the bifurcation behaviour of the uncoupled Izhikevich model itself. The accuracy of the prediction of the phase model is supported by simulations of two weakly coupled Izhikevich neurons.

AI.tldr: First computation of a phase model for the Izhikevich neuron with chemical synapses, enabling study of phase-locking states despite the model being a discontinuous dynamical system.
AI.motivation: The Izhikevich model is computationally efficient and reproduces diverse firing patterns, but as a discontinuous dynamical system it cannot be analyzed with weakly coupled oscillator theory designed for continuous systems, leaving its collective behavior under coupling largely unexplored.
AI.method: Compute the phase model for an Izhikevich neuron with chemical synapses, then use it to analyze existence and stability of phase-locking states and their parameter dependence. Link anti-phase state stability to the bifurcation behavior of the uncoupled Izhikevich model, validated by simulations of two weakly coupled neurons.
AI.result: Phase-locking states and their stability vary with parameters, and the stability of anti-phase states is connected to the bifurcation behavior of the uncoupled Izhikevich model. Predictions match simulations of two weakly coupled Izhikevich neurons.
AI.conclusion: A phase model for the synaptically coupled Izhikevich neuron is feasible and accurate, providing a bridge between discontinuous single-neuron dynamics and coupled collective behavior.

title: On non-monotonic steady state response curves
summary: Non-monotonic steady state response curves can readily arise from an incoherent feedforward loop (IFFL), which has also been conjectured to be a necessary mechanism. In a previous work, we showed this conjecture to be false for systems where the control parameter directly influences only one state variable. Here, we extend this result to arbitrary systems. We show that a stable non-monotonic response requires either an IFFL or a combination of positive and negative feedback loops. Finally, we apply our theoretical findings to three network-structured biological contexts: signaling pathways, gene regulation, and ecological consumer-resource models. For the first two contexts, we identify necessary motifs for non-monotonic responses, while for consumer-resource models, we provide an alternative proof of the Competitive Exclusion Principle.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes a prior result showing that IFFL is not necessary for non-monotonic steady-state responses, proving that such responses require either an IFFL or a mix of positive and negative feedback loops, and applies this to biological networks.
AI.motivation: Non-monotonic steady-state response curves are often thought to require an incoherent feedforward loop (IFFL) as a necessary mechanism, but the authors previously showed this conjecture fails when the control parameter affects only one state variable. This work aims to extend that finding to arbitrary systems.
AI.method: The authors generalize their earlier analysis to arbitrary systems, deriving conditions for stable non-monotonic responses. They then apply the theoretical results to three network-structured biological contexts: signaling pathways, gene regulation, and ecological consumer-resource models.
AI.result: A stable non-monotonic response requires either an IFFL or a combination of positive and negative feedback loops. For signaling pathways and gene regulation, the authors identify necessary motifs for non-monotonic responses; for consumer-resource models, they provide an alternative proof of the Competitive Exclusion Principle.
AI.conclusion: The IFFL is not the only mechanism for non-monotonic steady-state responses; feedback loop combinations also suffice. The framework yields motif requirements in biological networks and an alternative proof of the Competitive Exclusion Principle.

title: MEM as an Extension of Recurrent Processing Theory: Toward a Motivational Account of Consciousness
summary: Victor Lamme's Recurrent Processing Theory (RPT) proposes that the feedforward sweep (FFS) can extract and categorize visual features unconsciously, while conscious vision emerges through recurrent processing and feedback interactions across representational levels. The Motivated Emotional Mind (MEM) model, developed by Wiesław L. Galus and Janusz A. Starzyk, retains this core principle but embeds it in an embodied architecture integrating multilayer networks, semi-hierarchical semblions, receptors, effectors, allostasis, emotional valuation, and memory-based sensory reconstruction. This article examines the substantive but limited relationship between RPT and MEM. While RPT explains the role of recurrence in perceptual organization and the transition to conscious vision, MEM addresses the content of recurrent processing, its grounding in receptor activity and bodily states, its interaction with memory and action, and the possible role of reconstructed sensory representations in phenomenal experience. Particular emphasis is placed on secondary perception: the top-down reconstruction of sensory and interoceptive maps through which memories, mental imagery, dreams, hallucinations, feelings, and observed scenarios acquire experiential form. MEM thus associates phenomenality not merely with recurrent activity or reportability, but with the reconstruction of modality-specific, receptor-grounded sensory and bodily content. The article also presents the mathematical model of MEM, formalizing re-entrant processing, representational competition, allostasis, affect, curiosity, procedural gaps, and action selection. We conclude that MEM can be viewed as an embodied and motivational extension of RPT. However, its distinctive claims, particularly the sufficiency of secondary perception for phenomenality and the proposed microstructure of semblions, remain hypotheses requiring causal testing.

AI.tldr: This article compares Lamme's Recurrent Processing Theory (RPT) with the Motivated Emotional Mind (MEM) model, arguing MEM is an embodied, motivational extension of RPT, while noting MEM's distinctive claims remain untested hypotheses.
AI.motivation: To clarify the substantive but limited relationship between RPT and MEM, and to assess whether MEM extends RPT's account of recurrence into an embodied, motivational framework.
AI.method: Conceptual comparison of RPT and MEM, plus presentation of MEM's mathematical model formalizing re-entrant processing, representational competition, allostasis, affect, curiosity, procedural gaps, and action selection.
AI.result: RPT explains recurrence's role in perceptual organization and the transition to consciousness; MEM additionally addresses the content of recurrent processing, its grounding in receptors and bodily states, memory/action interaction, and the role of reconstructed sensory representations. Emphasis is placed on secondary perception as top-down reconstruction underlying memories, imagery, dreams, hallucinations, feelings, and observed scenarios.
AI.conclusion: MEM can be seen as an embodied and motivational extension of RPT, but its distinctive claims—especially the sufficiency of secondary perception for phenomenality and the proposed microstructure of semblions—remain hypotheses requiring causal testing.

title: Fluctuation theorems and exact multi-allele fixation probabilities
comment: 17 pages, 4 figures in the main text, 6 figures in the supplement
summary: A mutant gene that appears in a finite population will, in the long run, either disappear from it or become fixed, so that all members of the population will carry a copy of the mutant gene. Determining the fixation probability of a mutant gene is thus a prerequisite for modeling evolutionary dynamics in finite populations. Within the diffusion theory framework, the mutant's competition with the wild-type genes is described by the closed-form solution of a one-dimensional backward Kolmogorov equation for the mutant fixation probability, derived by Motoo Kimura in 1962. However, in asexual populations the rate of adaptation and the relative importance of alternative evolutionary pathways are shaped by clonal interference - the competition between several lineages arising from distinct beneficial or deleterious mutations. Quantitative descriptions of clonal interference require computing fixation probabilities in populations where multiple alleles are present simultaneously - a formidable mathematical problem which amounts to solving a multi-dimensional backward Kolmogorov equation. Here, we employ fluctuation theorems (a set of exact equalities in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics) in order to re-derive Kimura's fixation probability formula. When extended to multi-allele systems, fluctuation theorems provide a constraint which must be satisfied by any valid set of fixation probabilities. Moreover, we present a recursive analytical solution of the multi-allele fixation probability problem. We use our formalism to study the fate of a novel beneficial mutation in a clonal interference scenario, discovering substantial deviations between our exact treatment and the mean-field approximation in which the target mutation competes with a single effective genotype. Our formalism can be used to replace both explicit simulations and approximate analytical results in models of asexual evolution.

AI.tldr: The paper re-derives Kimura's fixation probability using fluctuation theorems and extends this to a recursive analytical solution for multi-allele fixation probabilities, enabling exact study of clonal interference.
AI.motivation: Determining fixation probability is essential for modeling evolutionary dynamics in finite populations. Kimura's diffusion-theory solution handles only a single mutant competing with wild-type. In asexual populations, adaptation depends on clonal interference among multiple lineages, requiring multi-dimensional backward Kolmogorov equations that are mathematically formidable.
AI.method: The authors employ fluctuation theorems from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics to re-derive Kimura's fixation probability formula, then extend them to multi-allele systems. They derive a constraint on valid fixation probability sets and present a recursive analytical solution of the multi-allele fixation probability problem.
AI.result: Applied to a novel beneficial mutation under clonal interference, the exact treatment shows substantial deviations from the mean-field approximation where the mutation competes with a single effective genotype.
AI.conclusion: The formalism can replace explicit simulations and approximate analytical results in models of asexual evolution.

title: Multimodal Physiological Decoding Reveals Individualized Arousal Dynamics in Closed-Loop Neurofeedback
summary: Most arousal-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) use EEG to decode cognitive state. But arousal is an autonomic process. We examined if peripheral physiological signals give a better decode of task-related arousal. We used a public dataset from a difficult boundary-avoidance flight task. In this task, participants received EEG-based BCI neurofeedback, sham feedback, or no feedback. We trained a multimodal deep learning decoder on heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), respiration, electrodermal activity, and pupil diameter. We compared it with an EEG-only decoder and with the original filter-bank common spatial pattern (FBCSP) decoder. All analyses were offline. The peripheral decoder had a within-subject AUC of 93.0%. The EEG-only decoder had 85.2% and the FBCSP decoder had 79.8%. Only the peripheral decoder showed the Yerkes-Dodson inverted-U relation between decoded arousal and performance. The feedback conditions did not change the arousal trajectories. Thus, the BCI benefit possibly comes from regulation at critical moments in the task, not from a continuous shift. We calculated a time-varying optimal arousal trajectory from control trials. Per-trial deviations from this trajectory predicted performance (r = -0.28 to -0.24, p < 0.01). Baseline HRV and gamma power changed the arousal-performance curve of each subject. We used these values to divide subjects into arousal-sensitive and arousal-tolerant groups. Control bands specific to each group increased trial separation (Cohen's d from 1.21 to 1.32 and from 0.85 to 1.10). These results show that peripheral signals are better than EEG for continuous arousal decoding. They also give a specification for individualized closed-loop arousal regulation. A prospective study must test this specification, for example with personalized transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation.

AI.tldr: Peripheral physiological signals outperform EEG for decoding task-related arousal, and individualized arousal trajectories and subject groupings can inform personalized closed-loop arousal regulation.
AI.motivation: Most arousal-based BCIs rely on EEG to decode cognitive state, but arousal is fundamentally an autonomic process, suggesting peripheral physiological signals may provide a better decode of task-related arousal.
AI.method: Using a public dataset from a difficult boundary-avoidance flight task (with neurofeedback, sham, or no feedback), they trained a multimodal deep learning decoder on heart rate, HRV, respiration, electrodermal activity, and pupil diameter, comparing it against EEG-only and FBCSP decoders. They also computed a time-varying optimal arousal trajectory, examined per-trial deviations, and used baseline HRV and gamma power to divide subjects into arousal-sensitive and arousal-tolerant groups.
AI.result: The peripheral decoder reached 93.0% within-subject AUC vs 85.2% (EEG-only) and 79.8% (FBCSP). Only the peripheral decoder showed the Yerkes-Dodson inverted-U relation. Feedback conditions did not change arousal trajectories. Per-trial deviations from the optimal trajectory predicted performance (r = -0.28 to -0.24, p < 0.01). Baseline HRV and gamma power modulated the arousal-performance curve, enabling group division; group-specific control bands increased trial separation (Cohen's d 1.21→1.32 and 0.85→1.10).
AI.conclusion: Peripheral signals outperform EEG for continuous arousal decoding and provide a specification for individualized closed-loop arousal regulation, which should be tested prospectively (e.g., via personalized transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation).

title: Beyond Completion Time: A Multimodal Approach to Characterizing Eye-Hand Coordination During the Nine-Hole Peg Test in Multiple Sclerosis
summary: Multiple sclerosis (MS) can impair upper-extremity function through motor, sensory, cognitive, and visual deficits. Although the Nine-Hole Peg Test (9-HPT) is widely used to assess dexterity, completion time alone provides limited insight into the eye-hand coordination underlying performance. We characterized 9-HPT performance in nine people with MS (PwMS) and nine healthy controls using simultaneous eye tracking, markerless hand tracking, and object detection. Each peg cycle was divided into transport, manipulation and insertion, and return-to-bin phases. PwMS had longer overall completion times. Transport was prolonged with the non-dominant hand, manipulation was prolonged with the dominant hand, and return-to-bin duration was longer with both hands, representing the largest phase difference. PwMS also made approximately one additional fixation per peg and showed greater variability in gaze landing position during dominant-hand performance. Saccadic amplitude and mean placement error did not differ significantly between groups, and gaze generally preceded hand movement in both groups. These exploratory findings suggest that MS-related slowing is concentrated in phases requiring precise manipulation and transition to the next peg. Multimodal assessment of the 9-HPT can reveal coordination deficits not captured by completion time alone.

AI.tldr: Using eye tracking, markerless hand tracking, and object detection, the study decomposed Nine-Hole Peg Test performance into phases, finding that MS-related slowing concentrates in manipulation and transition phases and is accompanied by more fixations and greater gaze variability, revealing coordination deficits invisible to completion time alone.
AI.motivation: The Nine-Hole Peg Test (9-HPT) is widely used to assess upper-extremity dexterity in multiple sclerosis, but completion time alone provides limited insight into the eye-hand coordination underlying performance. The authors aimed to characterize the coordination deficits that timing metrics miss.
AI.method: Nine people with MS (PwMS) and nine healthy controls performed the 9-HPT while being recorded with simultaneous eye tracking, markerless hand tracking, and object detection. Each peg cycle was segmented into transport, manipulation and insertion, and return-to-bin phases for analysis.
AI.result: PwMS had longer overall completion times. Transport was prolonged with the non-dominant hand, manipulation with the dominant hand, and return-to-bin with both hands (the largest phase difference). PwMS made about one additional fixation per peg and showed greater gaze landing variability during dominant-hand performance. Saccadic amplitude and mean placement error did not differ significantly, and gaze generally preceded hand movement in both groups.
AI.conclusion: Exploratory findings suggest MS-related slowing is concentrated in phases requiring precise manipulation and transition to the next peg. Multimodal assessment of the 9-HPT can reveal coordination deficits not captured by completion time alone.

title: A Unified Unsupervised Framework for Genome-Wide Association Studies in Heterogeneous Populations
summary: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have greatly advanced the discovery of genetic variants underlying complex traits and diseases. Yet in heterogeneous populations, existing GWAS strategies typically either pool all individuals under an assumption of population homogeneity or perform meta-analysis across predefined subgroups, both of which are limited when latent genetic heterogeneity attenuates subgroup-specific effects and masks true associations or subgroup labels are imprecise. Here we present UCALM, a unified unsupervised framework that infers genetically homogeneous subgroups directly from the data and integrates subgroup-specific GWAS with a novel layered meta-analysis method to capture both shared and subgroup-specific association signals. Through extensive simulations and analyses of large-scale human and livestock cohorts, including the UK Biobank ($n \approx 487{,}000$) and a heterogeneous pig cohort ($n \approx 85{,}000$), we demonstrate that UCALM substantially alleviated the mean genomic inflation across 24 UK Biobank traits to 1.17 compared with 1.43 for GLM and 1.37 for LDAK-KVIK, and further revealed 74 loci in the pig cohort that were previously obscured by conventional approaches. Our results establish a robust and broadly applicable strategy for association mapping in structured populations and improve the resolution of genetic signals across diverse species.

AI.tldr: UCALM is a unified unsupervised framework that infers genetically homogeneous subgroups directly from data and combines subgroup-specific GWAS with a layered meta-analysis to capture both shared and subgroup-specific association signals in heterogeneous populations.
AI.motivation: Existing GWAS strategies in heterogeneous populations either pool all individuals assuming homogeneity or meta-analyze predefined subgroups. Both are limited when latent genetic heterogeneity attenuates subgroup-specific effects (masking true associations) or when subgroup labels are imprecise.
AI.method: UCALM: an unsupervised framework inferring genetically homogeneous subgroups directly from the data, integrating subgroup-specific GWAS with a novel layered meta-analysis method to capture shared and subgroup-specific signals.
AI.result: Evaluated via extensive simulations and large-scale cohorts (UK Biobank n≈487,000; heterogeneous pig cohort n≈85,000). UCALM reduced mean genomic inflation across 24 UK Biobank traits to 1.17 vs. 1.43 for GLM and 1.37 for LDAK-KVIK, and revealed 74 loci in the pig cohort previously obscured by conventional approaches.
AI.conclusion: UCALM establishes a robust, broadly applicable strategy for association mapping in structured populations, improving resolution of genetic signals across diverse species.

title: Heterarchy in the Brain: Control as a Spectrum, Not a Chain of Command
summary: Neuroscience treats the brain as a control hierarchy, with cortical systems governing subcortical mechanisms. We argue that this mistakes a configuration for an architecture. Local asymmetries of influence are real, but control is relational and process-specific; because neural elements constrain one another across concurrent processes, relations can form cycles that resist a stable ranking. Evidence from learned action, cortico-cerebellar and thalamocortical loops, and defensive behavior shows that control changes with practice, task phase, urgency, viability demands, and affordances. Hierarchical order therefore characterizes time-bounded configurations, whereas heterarchy characterizes the architecture's repertoire across occasions. We propose a spectrum of control indexed by dynamical decoupling: how far behavior can depend on history, internal state, and anticipated consequences. The account yields experimentally testable predictions.

AI.tldr: The paper argues neuroscience mischaracterizes the brain: hierarchy (cortical-to-subcortical control) is only a transient configuration, while the underlying architecture is heterarchical. It proposes a control spectrum indexed by dynamical decoupling.
AI.motivation: Neuroscience widely treats the brain as a control hierarchy with cortical systems governing subcortical mechanisms. The authors contend this confuses a configuration for an architecture, overlooking that control is relational and process-specific, and that bidirectional constraints across concurrent processes can form cycles resistant to stable ranking.
AI.method: Conceptual/theoretical argument supported by evidence from learned action, cortico-cerebellar and thalamocortical loops, and defensive behavior, showing that control shifts with practice, task phase, urgency, viability demands, and affordances. The authors introduce a spectrum of control indexed by dynamical decoupling.
AI.result: Hierarchical order characterizes time-bounded configurations, whereas heterarchy characterizes the architecture's repertoire across occasions. Control varies along a spectrum reflecting how far behavior depends on history, internal state, and anticipated consequences.
AI.conclusion: Reconceiving the brain as heterarchical rather than strictly hierarchical yields experimentally testable predictions, offering a more accurate account of neural control organization.

title: Efficiency and robustness partition the solution space for memory in recurrent networks
summary: In computational neuroscience, task-trained recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are commonly used as a testbed for exploring the space of recurrent circuit solutions compatible with a particular function. However, these networks are subject to inductive biases that may be misaligned with those of biological circuits, which operate under various efficiency and robustness constraints. Here, using a minimal stimulus recall task, we systematically characterize how the solution space of recurrent neural networks is shaped by the desiderata of weight efficiency, activity efficiency, and robustness to noise. We show that weight efficient solutions exhibit a low-rank bias that aligns with the inductive biases of task-trained networks and favors dynamical motifs involving slow, persistent dynamics, whereas activity efficiency encourages high-rank solutions that rely on transient amplification. Moreover, we find that activity efficient solutions exhibit a strong dissociation between high-variance modes of activity and those that causally influence network output. Unlike in static feedforward settings, we demonstrate that noise robustness and activity efficiency are generally in opposition, rather than synergistic. Using these findings, we propose a normative account of misaligned coding phenomena recently identified in premotor cortex.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes how weight efficiency, activity efficiency, and noise robustness shape the solution space of task-trained RNNs, revealing opposing biases and offering a normative account of misaligned coding in premotor cortex.
AI.motivation: Task-trained RNNs are widely used to study recurrent circuit solutions, but they carry inductive biases potentially misaligned with biological circuits, which face efficiency and robustness constraints. The authors aim to systematically understand how these desiderata shape the solution space.
AI.method: Using a minimal stimulus recall task, they systematically characterize how the RNN solution space is shaped by weight efficiency, activity efficiency, and robustness to noise.
AI.result: Weight-efficient solutions show a low-rank bias matching task-trained network priors, favoring slow persistent dynamics; activity efficiency encourages high-rank solutions relying on transient amplification. Activity-efficient solutions dissociate high-variance activity modes from causally output-relevant ones. Noise robustness and activity efficiency are generally opposed, not synergistic as in static feedforward settings.
AI.conclusion: These findings provide a normative account of misaligned coding phenomena recently identified in premotor cortex.

title: Tracing model-generated DNA with position-independent watermarking
summary: Genomic language models can write synthetic DNA that carries no record of its origin. A generation-time watermark could provide a provenance signal, if a verifier can detect it using only the DNA sequence, a key, and published detector settings, without knowing where the generated region starts, which strand it lies on, or how it was divided into six-base tokens. We embed the SynthID tournament watermark in two genomic language models, Carbon and GENERator-v2. The verifier searches both strands, every start position, and four window lengths, and corrects its decision for the whole search. In a detection cohort of 1,544 held-out prompts, it found all 3,088 marked sequences per model, unedited and after one substituted, inserted, or deleted base. For ordinary sequences, the one-sided 95% upper confidence bound on the false-positive rate was at most 0.850%; one bound for the wrong-key control reached 1.015% (Carbon, after a deletion). In a development cohort, neither model showed a detectable change in likelihood or in predefined sequence measures. Under random edits placed without reference to the detector, detection stayed complete or nearly complete up to a 2% per-base edit rate. These results show statistical detection, not biological function, secret-key security, or robustness to an editor who sees the detector.

AI.tldr: The SynthID tournament watermark is embedded in two genomic language models; a verifier that searches both strands, all start positions, and four window lengths detects all marked sequences even after edits, with false-positive rates around 1%.
AI.motivation: Synthetic DNA from genomic language models carries no record of its origin, so a generation-time watermark could supply a provenance signal detectable from sequence, key, and published settings alone.
AI.method: Embed the SynthID tournament watermark in Carbon and GENERator-v2; the verifier searches both strands, every start position, and four window lengths, then corrects its decision for the full search.
AI.result: On 1,544 held-out prompts, all 3,088 marked sequences per model were found, unedited and after one substitution/insertion/deletion. False-positive one-sided 95% upper bound was at most 0.850% (wrong-key control up to 1.015%). No detectable likelihood or sequence-measure change in development cohort; detection remained complete or nearly complete up to 2% per-base random edit rate.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate statistical detection only—not biological function, secret-key security, or robustness to an adversary who can see the detector.

title: Integrated omics reveals actionable drivers of bioactive variation in US milk
summary: Despite milk being a global dietary staple, the molecular basis of its health-relevant bioactivity and the factors governing fine-scale compositional variation remain poorly understood. Here, we present an integrated seven-layer omics characterization of 60 US retail milk samples from ten geographic regions, combining genomics, transcriptomics, peptidomics, proteomics, lipidomics, metabolomics, and glycomics on the same samples. We also organized the identified and quantified compounds into the Dairy Molecule Database (DMD), a web-accessible resource for linking milk compound concentrations with SNPs, miRNAs, and product-level factors to support future milk quality optimization. In total, we identified 6,714 compounds and quantified 5,288 with absolute concentrations, including 5,220 compounds not previously available with absolute concentration estimates in existing milk compound databases. These profiles enabled bioactivity efficacy estimation and association analyses of factors linked to milk compound variation. We tested 54 computationally predicted antimicrobial candidate peptides; 35 showed activity and 6 had IC50 values below 256 μg/mL against A. baumannii, an ESKAPE pathogen. We further identified associations between downstream bioactive compound concentrations or estimated bioactivity efficacy and product-level factors, including purchase region, purchase ambient temperature, and packaging opacity, as well as SNPs, estimated Jersey breed proportion, and miRNA abundance. Overall, bioactivity efficacy profiles were associated with purchase region, selected SNPs, Jersey breed proportion, and selected miRNAs. These findings suggest that selective breeding and supply-chain optimization could help improve the bioactive quality of commercial milk.

AI.tldr: A seven-layer omics study of 60 US retail milk samples identified 6,714 compounds and revealed that milk's bioactive quality is linked to genetics, breed, and supply-chain factors, with potential for optimization through breeding and logistics.
AI.motivation: Despite milk being a global dietary staple, the molecular basis of its health-relevant bioactivity and the factors governing fine-scale compositional variation remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Integrated seven-layer omics characterization (genomics, transcriptomics, peptidomics, proteomics, lipidomics, metabolomics, glycomics) of 60 US retail milk samples from ten regions, along with organizing compounds into the Dairy Molecule Database (DMD) linking concentrations to SNPs, miRNAs, and product-level factors.
AI.result: Identified 6,714 compounds and quantified 5,288 with absolute concentrations (5,220 not previously available). Of 54 predicted antimicrobial peptides tested, 35 showed activity and 6 had IC50 <256 μg/mL against A. baumannii. Bioactive compound concentrations and efficacy were associated with purchase region, ambient temperature, packaging opacity, SNPs, Jersey breed proportion, and miRNA abundance.
AI.conclusion: Selective breeding and supply-chain optimization could help improve the bioactive quality of commercial milk.

title: Approximating Parameter Regions for Multistationarity and Multistability in Mass-Action Systems
summary: Identifying kinetic parameters and conserved quantities that support multistationarity and multistability remains challenging in chemical reaction network analysis. Structural theory provides existence and exclusion results, but does not always yield explicit, interpretable descriptions of the corresponding parameter regimes. We present a computational and machine-learning framework for discovering and characterizing parameter regimes with numerical evidence of multistationarity and multistability in mass-action systems. We refer to these numerically detected behaviors as approximate multistationarity and approximate multistability. The framework combines Latin hypercube sampling, adaptive sampling, and interpretable surrogate modeling. Logistic-regression and neural-network surrogates are trained separately on accumulated detection labels and independently guide later sampling toward regions with high scores for approximate multistationarity or multistability. Boundary refinement targets transitions between detected and undetected numerical classes. Buckingham--Pi groups are then used with CN2 rule induction to obtain interpretable empirical descriptions of detected regimes. Illustrative networks yield rules consistent with known multistationarity conditions, while the Schlögl model demonstrates adaptive enrichment of multistationarity detections. In the hybrid histidine kinase model and the sequential dual phosphorylation cycle, adaptive sampling substantially increased the number of parameter - total pairs with detected multistability relative to global sampling under equal sampling budgets. The framework complements analytical chemical reaction network theory by providing efficient, parameter-resolved discovery and characterization of multistationary and multistable regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a computational and machine-learning framework to discover and characterize parameter regimes exhibiting numerical evidence of multistationarity and multistability in mass-action chemical reaction networks.
AI.motivation: Identifying kinetic parameters and conserved quantities supporting multistationarity/multistability is challenging. Structural theory gives existence and exclusion results but rarely explicit, interpretable parameter regimes.
AI.method: Combines Latin hypercube sampling, adaptive sampling, and interpretable surrogate modeling (logistic regression and neural networks) trained on detection labels to guide sampling. Boundary refinement targets class transitions. Buckingham-Pi groups with CN2 rule induction yield interpretable empirical descriptions.
AI.result: Illustrative networks yield rules consistent with known multistationarity conditions; the Schlögl model shows adaptive enrichment of multistationarity detections. In the hybrid histidine kinase model and sequential dual phosphorylation cycle, adaptive sampling substantially increased detected multistability parameter pairs versus global sampling under equal budgets.
AI.conclusion: The framework complements analytical chemical reaction network theory by providing efficient, parameter-resolved discovery and characterization of multistationary and multistable regimes.

title: Recurrent network dynamics explain the time course of perceptual grouping in natural scenes
summary: How the brain groups image elements into coherent objects in natural scenes remains unclear. Existing models for grouping in biological vision rely on simplified stimuli with explicit boundaries and cannot explain human behavior in naturalistic settings. We propose a mechanistic framework in which recurrent interactions propagate enhanced neuronal activity within and between cortical areas. The framework links computational principles, neural circuitry and perceptual psychology. Local boundary signals govern early grouping, whereas later stages integrate top-down feedback carrying information about object identity, grouping features across internal edges into coherent object representations. We instantiated this framework as a brain-inspired recurrent neural network trained to group features in natural images. The network learned to propagate enhanced activity across a cued object's representation, mirroring the brain's perceptual grouping mechanisms. The network's dynamics also predicted human reaction times. The framework links cortical dynamics to human vision and generates testable predictions for neuro-physiological and psychophysical experiments.

AI.tldr: A brain-inspired recurrent neural network framework explains how the brain groups image elements into coherent objects, linking cortical dynamics to human perception.
AI.motivation: Existing models of perceptual grouping in biological vision rely on simplified stimuli with explicit boundaries, failing to explain human behavior in naturalistic scenes. It remains unclear how the brain groups image elements into coherent objects in natural scenes.
AI.method: The authors propose a mechanistic framework where recurrent interactions propagate enhanced neuronal activity within and between cortical areas. Local boundary signals govern early grouping, while later stages integrate top-down feedback carrying object identity information to group features across internal edges. They instantiated this as a brain-inspired recurrent neural network trained to group features in natural images.
AI.result: The network learned to propagate enhanced activity across a cued object's representation, mirroring the brain's perceptual grouping mechanisms. Its dynamics also predicted human reaction times.
AI.conclusion: The framework links cortical dynamics to human vision and generates testable predictions for neurophysiological and psychophysical experiments.

title: A multimodal computer-vision based pipeline for eye-hand coordination quantification during the Nine-Hole Peg Test
summary: The Nine-Hole Peg Test (9-HPT) is a widely used clinical measure of manual dexterity in multiple sclerosis (MS), but its primary outcome, task completion time, provides limited information about the visuomotor mechanisms contributing to impaired performance. Instrumented approaches can provide richer kinematic information but often require modifications to the task or physical instrumentation that may alter natural hand-object interaction. We developed a multimodal computer-vision pipeline that enables synchronized analysis of gaze, hand kinematics, and object state during an unmodified 9-HPT. Gaze was recorded using Pupil Labs Invisible glasses, three-dimensional hand landmarks were reconstructed using WiLoR, and a custom YOLO26x-seg model detected and tracked the pegboard, holes, pegs, and collection bin. Eye-tracking, hand, and object data were temporally synchronized at the video-frame level and spatially registered to a common pegboard-centered coordinate system using frame-specific projective transformations. The pipeline further integrated hole-state transitions, hand-zone classification, and fingertip kinematics to identify PICK and PLACE events and segment hand transport and stationary phases, while fixation and saccade labels were derived from the eye-tracking system. Automated detections were visually reviewed and corrected when necessary. The resulting framework provides synchronized, event-resolved measures of gaze behavior, hand movement, object interaction, and eye-hand coordination while preserving standardized 9-HPT administration. This approach extends the 9-HPT beyond completion time and provides a reproducible platform for investigating the visuomotor mechanisms underlying dexterity impairment in MS and other neurological disorders.

AI.tldr: A multimodal computer-vision pipeline enables synchronized analysis of gaze, hand kinematics, and object state during an unmodified Nine-Hole Peg Test, providing event-resolved visuomotor measures beyond simple completion time.
AI.motivation: The 9-HPT is a standard clinical dexterity measure in MS, but its completion-time outcome reveals little about the visuomotor mechanisms behind impaired performance. Existing instrumented methods add physical instrumentation or modify the task, potentially altering natural hand-object interaction.
AI.method: Gaze was recorded with Pupil Labs Invisible glasses; 3D hand landmarks were reconstructed with WiLoR; a custom YOLO26x-seg model detected and tracked the pegboard, holes, pegs, and bin. Eye-tracking, hand, and object data were synchronized at the video-frame level and spatially registered to a pegboard-centered coordinate system via frame-specific projective transformations. Hole-state transitions, hand-zone classification, and fingertip kinematics identified PICK/PLACE events and segmented transport and stationary phases; fixation/saccade labels came from the eye tracker. Detections were visually reviewed and corrected.
AI.result: The framework yields synchronized, event-resolved measures of gaze behavior, hand movement, object interaction, and eye-hand coordination, all while preserving standardized 9-HPT administration.
AI.conclusion: The approach extends the 9-HPT beyond completion time and offers a reproducible platform for studying visuomotor mechanisms of dexterity impairment in MS and other neurological disorders.

title: How Simple Models Can Reproduce Multiple Epidemic Waves: Peak Topology, Minimal Dynamic Complexity, and Inference for Time-Varying Transmission
summary: Multiple epidemic waves are often taken as evidence that simple compartmental models are structurally inadequate. Yet the key question is not whether a simple model can reproduce multiple peaks, but how much time-varying structure is minimally required to preserve observed epidemic-wave patterns and what can legitimately be inferred from such a representation. Using the susceptible-infectious-removed (SIR) model, we develop a framework for peak-preserving dynamic parsimony linking dynamical systems, inverse problems, statistical inference, and infectious-disease modeling. We establish exact multi-wave representability under time-varying transmission, characterize conditions for epidemic peaks and resurgence, and show the incidence-only non-identifiability of time-varying transmission and removal rates. Our main methodological contribution is minimal peak-preserving complexity (MPPC): the smallest dimension of a positive time-varying transmission function whose posterior-predictive trajectories preserve salient features, including peak count, timing, height, trough depth, and whole-curve agreement. We estimate MPPC using peak-aware approximate Bayesian computation and evaluate it through six reproducible stress tests, a Philippine COVID-19 reported-case proof of concept, and short-term future-knot projection. Across diverse data-generating mechanisms, low-dimensional time-varying SIR models can preserve aggregate epidemic-wave topology with modest dynamic complexity. However, accurate trajectory compression does not imply recovery of the underlying mechanism or reliable long-term counterfactual prediction. The framework therefore separates four often-conflated questions: representability, minimal dynamic complexity, mechanistic identifiability, and projection validity, providing a basis for parsimonious modeling of complex epidemic trajectories.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework for "minimal peak-preserving complexity" (MPPC) in time-varying SIR models, showing that low-dimensional time-varying transmission can reproduce multi-wave epidemic patterns without implying mechanistic recovery or reliable long-term prediction.
AI.motivation: Multiple epidemic waves are often cited as evidence that simple compartmental models are structurally inadequate. The authors reframe the question: rather than asking whether a simple model can reproduce multiple peaks, they ask how much time-varying structure is minimally required to preserve observed wave patterns and what can legitimately be inferred from such representations.
AI.method: Using the SIR model, they develop a peak-preserving dynamic parsimony framework linking dynamical systems, inverse problems, statistical inference, and infectious-disease modeling. They establish exact multi-wave representability, characterize peak/resurgence conditions, and show incidence-only non-identifiability of time-varying transmission and removal rates. MPPC is estimated via peak-aware approximate Bayesian computation, evaluated through six reproducible stress tests, a Philippine COVID-19 proof of concept, and short-term future-knot projection.
AI.result: Across diverse data-generating mechanisms, low-dimensional time-varying SIR models can preserve aggregate epidemic-wave topology (peak count, timing, height, trough depth, whole-curve agreement) with modest dynamic complexity. However, accurate trajectory compression does not imply recovery of the underlying mechanism or reliable long-term counterfactual prediction.
AI.conclusion: The framework separates four often-conflated questions—representability, minimal dynamic complexity, mechanistic identifiability, and projection validity—providing a principled basis for parsimonious modeling of complex epidemic trajectories.

title: Stochastic evolutionary dynamics in structured populations: Network degree governs evolutionary stability
summary: Stochasticity shapes evolutionary dynamics in finite populations beyond the reach of infinite-population theories. Using a stochastic birth--death framework on random regular networks, we establish evolutionary stability criteria for finite structured populations playing three-strategy games and identify critical degree thresholds governing invasion dynamics. Our framework goes beyond two-strategy evolutionary games to reveal that the initial composition of multi-type mutants, together with population structure and stochasticity, shapes the evolutionary fate of the resident population.

AI.tldr: This paper develops stochastic evolutionary stability criteria for finite structured populations playing three-strategy games on random regular networks, identifying critical degree thresholds that govern invasion dynamics.
AI.motivation: Infinite-population theories cannot capture stochasticity in finite populations, and existing work largely focuses on two-strategy games, leaving multi-strategy evolutionary dynamics in finite structured populations underexplored.
AI.method: A stochastic birth-death framework on random regular networks is used to derive evolutionary stability criteria for finite structured populations playing three-strategy games and to identify critical degree thresholds.
AI.result: Critical degree thresholds governing invasion dynamics are identified, extending stability analysis beyond two-strategy games to three-strategy settings.
AI.conclusion: The initial composition of multi-type mutants, combined with population structure and stochasticity, shapes the evolutionary fate of the resident population in finite structured populations.

title: From communication to computation in neurons-on-a-chip: an in silico study of neurotopomorphic computing
summary: Living neuronal networks transform inputs through recurrent cellular and population dynamics, yet it is unknown which network architecture supports which computation. Neurons-on-a-chip turn this question into a design problem because microchannels guide axonal growth and set the network architecture. We introduce IC$^3$, an Integrated Characterisation of Communication-Driven Computation, which characterizes network state through neuronal dynamics, functional communication, and structural support. We implemented nine architectures \textit{in silico} as conductance-based spiking networks and tested each on frequency decoding, temporal-order discrimination, and fading memory. Predominantly feedforward circuits decoded best. Sequential Chain and Microchannel Diode had the lowest IC$^3$ and recruited a third of reachable neurons, yet achieved the two highest scores on both classification tasks. Across architectures, higher IC$^3$ went with lower classification scores. We term this new direction \emph{neurotopomorphic computing}, in which the physical organisation of neuronal connectivity is engineered as part of the computing substrate.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces IC$^3$, a framework characterizing communication-driven computation in neurons-on-a-chip, and shows that specific microchannel-guided architectures (Sequential Chain, Microchannel Diode) outperform others on classification despite using fewer neurons.
AI.motivation: It is unknown which network architecture supports which computation in living neuronal networks. Neurons-on-a-chip allow this to become a design problem since microchannels guide axonal growth and set architecture.
AI.method: The authors introduce IC$^3$ (Integrated Characterisation of Communication-Driven Computation), characterizing network state via neuronal dynamics, functional communication, and structural support. They implemented nine architectures in silico as conductance-based spiking networks and tested each on frequency decoding, temporal-order discrimination, and fading memory.
AI.result: Predominantly feedforward circuits decoded best. Sequential Chain and Microchannel Diode had the lowest IC$^3$ and recruited a third of reachable neurons, yet achieved the two highest scores on both classification tasks. Across architectures, higher IC$^3$ correlated with lower classification scores.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose a new direction termed neurotopomorphic computing, in which the physical organization of neuronal connectivity is engineered as part of the computing substrate.

title: APOD: reasoning-guided agentic population ordinary differential equation discovery for pharmacological digital twins
summary: Establishing ordinary differential equations (ODEs) describing population data is a fundamental part of mathematical modeling in pharmacology, crucial to developing digital twins. However, doing so from sparse, noisy data is a slow, expert-driven task. Existing automated methods either search a restricted model space or ignore population inter-individual variability. Here we introduce APOD (Agentic Population ODE Discovery), a language-model agent that iteratively reasons over biological knowledge and fit diagnostics in an open-ended search space to discover a population digital twin (PDT), i.e., a shared ODE system with between-subject variability. On synthetic pharmacokinetic and tumor-dynamics benchmarks, APOD recovered ground-truth structures in 94-100\% of runs, 12-fold faster in median than an established library-based search. On real cohorts it converged to valid structures, and proposed a PDT of radioligand-therapy-induced platelet dynamics that predicts thrombocytopenia from first-cycle data and simulates alternative dosing schedules that lower the predicted risk of toxicity.

AI.tldr: APOD is a language-model agent that discovers population digital twins (shared ODE systems with between-subject variability) from sparse noisy data, achieving 94-100% ground-truth recovery on benchmarks and enabling clinical dose-schedule simulation.
AI.motivation: Establishing ODEs for population data is fundamental to pharmacology digital twins, but doing so from sparse, noisy data is slow and expert-driven. Existing automated methods either search a restricted model space or ignore population inter-individual variability.
AI.method: Introduces APOD (Agentic Population ODE Discovery), a language-model agent that iteratively reasons over biological knowledge and fit diagnostics within an open-ended search space to discover a population digital twin—a shared ODE system with between-subject variability.
AI.result: On synthetic pharmacokinetic and tumor-dynamics benchmarks, APOD recovered ground-truth structures in 94-100% of runs, 12-fold faster in median than a library-based search. On real cohorts it converged to valid structures.
AI.conclusion: APOD proposed a PDT of radioligand-therapy-induced platelet dynamics that predicts thrombocytopenia from first-cycle data and simulates alternative dosing schedules that lower predicted toxicity risk.

title: Measles transmission and surveillance in open subcommunities
summary:
We're often in a situation where we have models of measles transmission that are stuck at a coarse population scale. This paper is about increasing their resolution or, said differently, creating consistent models for the population's subcommunities. We pay special attention to the fact that even if the full population is isolated, subcommunities are open to measles importations and related consequences of population movement.
  It turns out that the resolution issue can be productively framed as a constrained optimization problem, where the constraint is aggregation to the coarse model. That mathematical scaffolding allows us to make epidemiologically motivated approximations concentrated at the large population scale, where they're more valid, which leaves the estimates at the fine subcommunity scale atypically unstructured.
  We develop the idea in the context of the pre-vaccination-era 60 city UK dataset, building transmission models for all 60 cities. We find that they have intuitive seasonality, volatility, and importation elements, but that they depend on nontrivial dynamics in their case reporting probabilities. Potential interpretations of those surveillance processes are discussed in some detail, and we also describe how they influence inference on the balance between competing cryptic transmission and transient elimination dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes framing the problem of increasing the resolution of coarse-scale measles transmission models as a constrained optimization problem, where the constraint is aggregation to the coarse model, enabling consistent subcommunity-level models.
AI.motivation: Existing measles transmission models are often stuck at a coarse population scale. There is a need to increase their resolution and create consistent models for subcommunities, especially accounting for the fact that even isolated populations have subcommunities open to measles importations and population movement effects.
AI.method: The resolution issue is framed as a constrained optimization problem with aggregation to the coarse model as the constraint. This scaffolding allows epidemiologically motivated approximations concentrated at the large population scale (where they are more valid), leaving fine subcommunity-scale estimates atypically unstructured. The approach is developed using the pre-vaccination-era 60 city UK dataset, building transmission models for all 60 cities.
AI.result: The resulting models exhibit intuitive seasonality, volatility, and importation elements, but depend on nontrivial dynamics in their case reporting probabilities. These surveillance processes influence inference on the balance between competing cryptic transmission and transient elimination dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The constrained optimization framing productively resolves the model resolution issue. Potential interpretations of the surveillance/reporting processes are discussed in detail, along with how they affect inference on cryptic transmission versus transient elimination dynamics.

title: COMPASS 2.0: psychometric representational similarity analysis distinguishes symptom structure from personal signal
comment: 28 pages, including Extended Data and Supplementary Information. Code for reproducibility: https://github.com/linlab/xpsych
summary: Language models can score psychiatric questionnaires from speech, but agreement with self-report may reflect the questionnaire rather than the person. We introduce psychometric representational similarity analysis, a framework for comparing the structure of speech-derived scores, self-report, item wording and theory, and implement it alongside person-level construct scoring in COMPASS 2.0. We show how similarly worded items induce covariance without psychological signal. In pre-registered discovery and confirmation analyses of clinical interviews from 275 participants, language-derived symptom geometry resembled wording more than self-report, with no structure beyond wording detected by the registered tests. Geometric agreement with self-report survived assigning participants someone else's answers, whereas person-paired scores captured distress more than specific symptoms. Complementary analyses examined counselling quality and wording structure across 34 instruments and the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) framework. These findings distinguish agreement about psychological structure from evidence that language-derived assessments track individual people.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces psychometric representational similarity analysis (psychometric RSA) and COMPASS 2.0 to test whether speech-derived language model scores actually track individuals or merely reflect questionnaire wording structure. Across 275 participants, language-derived symptom geometry resembled item wording more than self-report, and geometric agreement with self-report persisted even with mismatched participants, while person-paired scores captured general distress rather than specific symptoms.
AI.motivation: Language models can score psychiatric questionnaires from speech, but agreement with self-report may reflect the questionnaire's structure (e.g., wording similarity) rather than genuine psychological signal about the person. The authors aim to disentangle agreement about psychological structure from evidence that language-derived assessments track individual people.
AI.method: They propose psychometric representational similarity analysis, a framework comparing the structure of speech-derived scores, self-report, item wording, and theory, implemented alongside person-level construct scoring in COMPASS 2.0. They run pre-registered discovery and confirmation analyses on clinical interviews from 275 participants, including tests where participants were assigned someone else's answers, and complementary analyses of counselling quality and wording structure across 34 instruments and the RDoC framework.
AI.result: Language-derived symptom geometry resembled item wording more than self-report, with no structure beyond wording detected by the registered tests. Geometric agreement with self-report survived mismatching participants' answers, whereas person-paired scores captured distress more than specific symptoms. Similarly worded items induced covariance without psychological signal.
AI.conclusion: Apparent agreement between language-derived and self-report psychiatric scores can reflect questionnaire wording structure rather than person-level tracking. The findings caution against interpreting structural agreement as evidence that language-derived assessments capture individual people, and offer a framework to separate the two.

title: Interplay between Excitability and Noise in Analog Spiking Neurons
comment: Accepted for presentation at IEEE CDC 2026
summary: A spiking neuron is a dynamical system exhibiting a limit cycle (a spike) when subject to sufficiently excitatory input. Famous neuroscience experiments by Bryant and Segundo as well as Mainen and Sejnowski revealed that the spike times of some biological neurons are more reliable when subject to time-varying stimuli compared to constant ones. Provided with an industrial physics-based transient noise SPICE simulation framework compatible with foundry transistor compact models, we have demonstrated similar behaviours for a CMOS analog spiking neuron designed for neuromorphic computing hardware platforms. Under constant excitation current, the neuron operates in oscillatory regime and the empirical periods (interspike intervals) suffer from accumulated phase noise (jitter) during successive cycles, mainly due to the thermal noise of transistors. A time-varying input is reported to be capable of triggering output spikes according to a controlled statetransition mechanism, thereby significantly reducing the spike time jitter in the excitability regime. The physical limitation of the oscillatory or rate-coding regime in terms of reliabilitydissipation tradeoff is further evidenced by a stochastic thermodynamic uncertainty relation, a theorem that applies to general overdamped dissipative stochastic dynamical systems.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that a CMOS analog spiking neuron shows reduced spike-time jitter under time-varying stimulation compared to constant excitation, mirroring biological neuron reliability, and links this behavior to a thermodynamic uncertainty relation.
AI.motivation: Biological experiments (Bryant & Segundo; Mainen & Sejnowski) showed that some biological neurons fire more reliably with time-varying stimuli than with constant ones. The authors wanted to test whether a CMOS analog spiking neuron used in neuromorphic hardware exhibits similar reliability behavior.
AI.method: The authors used an industrial physics-based transient noise SPICE simulation framework compatible with foundry transistor compact models to study a CMOS analog spiking neuron. They compared constant excitation (oscillatory regime) with time-varying input (excitability regime) and analyzed jitter from transistor thermal noise.
AI.result: Under constant excitation current, the neuron oscillates with interspike intervals degraded by accumulated phase noise (jitter) from transistor thermal noise. A time-varying input triggers output spikes via a controlled state-transition mechanism, significantly reducing spike-time jitter in the excitability regime.
AI.conclusion: The physical limitation of the oscillatory/rate-coding regime in terms of a reliability-dissipation tradeoff is further evidenced by a stochastic thermodynamic uncertainty relation applicable to general overdamped dissipative stochastic dynamical systems.

title: Image-Based Breast Implant Detection for Mammography Dataset Curation and Near-Real-Time Deployment: Comparing Foundation Models and Task-Specific Convolutional Models
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine
summary: Purpose: To evaluate the performance-feasibility tradeoffs of foundation models (FMs) and task-specific convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained from scratch for breast implant classification in 2D mammography, with emphasis on suitability for near real-time clinical deployment. Methods: We evaluated four models: two FMs (RAD-DINO and MammoCLIP) and two CNNs trained from scratch for implant prediction (ResNet18 and our lightweight ResNetLite). Using the Emory Breast Imaging Dataset, 5,000 unilateral screening mammograms were used for training/validation and 1,000 manually reviewed unilateral images were held out for testing. For the FMs, global image embeddings from the pretrained encoder were classified using a support vector machine (SVM). The CNNs were trained end-to-end on 2D mammograms, with ResNetLite optimized via grid search over depth and width to balance accuracy and efficiency. Performance was evaluated using AUROC, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, embedding visualization, and inference-latency. Results: All models demonstrated strong performance on held-out test data (n = 1,000). MammoCLIP achieved the highest AUROC (0.999) with the quickest training time of 493 seconds. RAD-DINO achieved the highest sensitivity (0.980; accuracy 0.989) but had the slowest inference and training times. ResNet18 and MammoCLIP achieved comparable accuracy (0.985). ResNetLite showed no statistically significant difference from ResNet18 (AUROC 0.993; accuracy 0.976) despite using only 1.4% of ResNet18's parameters, and had the fastest inference time. Conclusion: FMs and task-specific CNN models reliably detect breast implants on 2D mammography.
