Model selection is best guided by deployment context: MammoCLIP for GPU-equipped hospital settings requiring scalable integration, and lightweight CNNs such as ResNetLite for resource-constrained or edge deployments.

AI.tldr: This study compares foundation models (FMs) and task-specific CNNs for breast implant classification in 2D mammography, evaluating accuracy vs. deployment efficiency. MammoCLIP achieved top AUROC (0.999), RAD-DINO highest sensitivity (0.980), while ResNetLite matched ResNet18 using only 1.4% of its parameters with fastest inference.
AI.motivation: To evaluate the performance-feasibility tradeoffs between foundation models and task-specific CNNs trained from scratch, with emphasis on suitability for near real-time clinical deployment of breast implant classification in 2D mammography.
AI.method: Four models were evaluated: two FMs (RAD-DINO, MammoCLIP) and two CNNs (ResNet18, lightweight ResNetLite). Using the Emory Breast Imaging Dataset, 5,000 unilateral screening mammograms were used for training/validation and 1,000 manually reviewed images for testing. FMs used SVM classification on global image embeddings; CNNs were trained end-to-end, with ResNetLite optimized via grid search. Evaluation used AUROC, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, embedding visualization, and inference latency.
AI.result: All models performed strongly on the held-out test set (n=1,000). MammoCLIP had the highest AUROC (0.999) and fastest training (493s). RAD-DINO had the highest sensitivity (0.980; accuracy 0.989) but slowest inference/training. ResNet18 and MammoCLIP had comparable accuracy (0.985). ResNetLite was statistically indistinguishable from ResNet18 (AUROC 0.993; accuracy 0.976) using only 1.4% of ResNet18's parameters, with the fastest inference.
AI.conclusion: Both FMs and task-specific CNNs reliably detect breast implants on 2D mammography. Model selection should be guided by deployment context: MammoCLIP for GPU-equipped hospital settings requiring scalable integration, and lightweight CNNs like ResNetLite for resource-constrained or edge deployments.

title: The Score Is Not the Structure: Brain Alignment and Cross-Lingual Transfer
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 - Linguistic Principles for Foundation Models (LP4FM). Code: https://github.com/saman-rahbar/score-is-not-the-structure
summary: Researchers often support the claim that a model shares structure with the brain, or across languages, by reporting a similarity score. We ask what such a score reads when the shared structure is absent, or when the tool that measures it does not work. We check two settings, and in both the score is not what it appears. First, a probe trained to tell grammatical from ungrammatical sentences in one language transfers worse to more distant languages, the usual evidence for shared structure. But the probe itself gets worse along the same axis: in four of seventeen languages it performs at chance, so 64 of 272 language pairs are scored with a tool that does not work. Dropping those languages halves the strength of the relationship, but they are also the most distant, and this design cannot separate the two effects. Counting matters too: the same data give p = 0.0006 when the 272 pairs are treated as independent and p = 0.155 when the seventeen languages are, which is the correct unit. Second, training a language model to match human brain responses raises its similarity score from 0.10 to 0.34, against a ceiling of 0.54. A model trained on a target whose correspondence to the brain was destroyed still scores 0.31, so only 0.028 to 0.068 of the rise is specific to the brain. With no model at all, a destroyed target already sits at 0.204 from the real one, a floor that tracks the target's rank divided by the number of sentences. Finally, steering a language along its own direction works (+6.2 over a random direction in sixteen of seventeen languages) yet shows no effect that varies with language distance. Before asking whether a correspondence helps, ask how much of the score would survive without it.

AI.tldr: Similarity scores used as evidence for shared structure (across languages or between models and brains) are often misleading: much of the score survives even when the shared structure is absent or the measuring tool fails.
AI.motivation: Researchers routinely claim a model shares structure with the brain or across languages by reporting a similarity score, but it is unclear what such a score actually reads when the shared structure is absent or when the measuring tool itself does not work.
AI.method: Two settings are examined. (1) Cross-lingual probes trained to distinguish grammatical from ungrammatical sentences, tested for transfer across 272 language pairs. (2) Language models trained to match human brain responses, compared against destroyed controls and a no-model floor. The authors test whether scores drop appropriately, how the unit of analysis (pairs vs. languages) affects significance, and whether steering along a language's own direction varies with language distance.
AI.result: Probes perform at chance in 4 of 17 languages, so 64 of 272 pairs are scored with a broken tool; dropping these halves the effect, but they are also the most distant, confounding the two. Significance flips from p=0.0006 (pairs as independent) to p=0.155 (languages, the correct unit). Brain-similarity rises from 0.10 to 0.34 (ceiling 0.54), but a destroyed target still scores 0.31, so only 0.028–0.068 is brain-specific; the no-model floor is 0.204. Steering along own direction helps (+6.2 over random in 16/17 languages) but shows no effect varying with language distance.
AI.conclusion: Reported similarity scores can largely survive the absence of the shared structure they are meant to evidence. Before asking whether a correspondence helps, researchers must ask how much of the score would remain without it; unit-of-analysis choices and broken tools further inflate apparent effects.

title: Cooperation thrives when moral judgment matches moral conduct
comment: Main text (27 pages, 4 figures, 4 Extended Data figures) and Supplementary Information (90 pages) in one PDF. Code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21519395
summary: A leading explanation for why humans cooperate with strangers is indirect reciprocity: when conduct is observed, individuals earn good reputations by cooperating with the deserving. Previous research has identified many "moral systems" that sustain cooperation through indirect reciprocity - each pairing a strategy for how to act with a norm for how to judge others - yet what makes them succeed, and whether that success generalizes beyond the donation game, has remained unclear. Here we evaluate all 1,048,576 moral systems whose norms condition on both players' reputations and actions, across every two-player social dilemma. We find that every highly stable, cooperative system pairs a "discriminating" strategy - one that cooperates with the good and defects against the bad when in good standing - with a "consistent" norm that deems good exactly those who act as the strategy prescribes. Such systems "practice what they preach" and preach what they practice. In the limit of small errors, only one strategy paired with a consistent norm remains stable across all social dilemmas: the "contrite discriminator", which cooperates to make amends when its standing is bad. Our results unify decades of research on indirect reciprocity, revealing moral consistency as the common ingredient of every stable, cooperative moral system.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates all 1,048,576 moral systems for indirect reciprocity across every two-player social dilemma, finding that stable cooperation requires pairing a "discriminating" strategy with a "consistent" norm, and that the "contrite discriminator" is uniquely stable under small errors.
AI.motivation: Indirect reciprocity explains human cooperation with strangers, but it was unclear what makes the many identified "moral systems" succeed and whether this success generalizes beyond the donation game.
AI.method: The authors exhaustively evaluate all 1,048,576 moral systems whose norms condition on both players' reputations and actions, across every two-player social dilemma, including a small-error limit analysis.
AI.result: Every highly stable, cooperative system pairs a "discriminating" strategy (cooperate with the good, defect against the bad when in good standing) with a "consistent" norm (deem good exactly those who act as the strategy prescribes). In the small-error limit, only the "contrite discriminator"—which cooperates to make amends when its standing is bad—remains stable across all dilemmas.
AI.conclusion: These results unify decades of indirect reciprocity research, revealing moral consistency as the common ingredient of every stable, cooperative moral system.

title: Exact and asymptotic enumeration of unrestricted binary phylogenetic networks through automorphism weights
summary: Let $\cP_{\ell,k}$ be the set of rooted binary phylogenetic networks with $\ell$ labelled leaves, $k$ reticulations and no parallel edges. We write $|\cP_{\ell,k}|=W_k(\ell)+D_k(\ell)$, where the weighted count $W_k(\ell)$ adds the inverse orders of the leaf-fixing automorphism groups and the defect $D_k(\ell)$ collects the remainder. The weighted count satisfies, for every $k$, a recursion over the source layers of the tree-component structure that involves neither a list of component graphs nor any distinction between symmetric and asymmetric configurations, and its exponential generating function is a Laurent polynomial in $\sqrt{1-2x}$. Automorphism groups of networks are $2$-groups, elementary abelian for $k\le5$ but not in general. For $k\le5$ the defect is the weighted count of networks with a distinguished involution, which obeys an extension of the same recursion. An exact symbolic evaluation of the two recursions yields $|\cP_{\ell,k}|$ in closed form for $k\le5$, the case $k=5$ being new; it reproduces the published counts for $k\le4$ and corrects a coefficient in a published generating function for $k=3$. For every $k$, uniformly over explicit ranges of $k$, we prove that the non-tree-child networks are a fraction $2k(k-1)/\ell$ of the tree-child networks to leading order, which gives the third term of the asymptotic expansion of $|\cP_{\ell,k}|$. We also prove that reticulation-visible networks exceed tree-child networks by the fraction $k(k-1)/\ell$, and that a uniformly random network in $\cP_{\ell,k}$ has a nontrivial automorphism with probability $k(k-1)/(4\ell^3)$ to leading order.

AI.tldr: The paper studies rooted binary phylogenetic networks with ℓ leaves and k reticulations, decomposing counts into a weighted part W_k(ℓ) and a defect D_k(ℓ), derives recursions via tree-component source layers, and gives closed-form totals for k≤5 plus asymptotic results on non-tree-child, reticulation-visible, and automorphism fractions.
AI.motivation: Counting rooted binary phylogenetic networks with given leaves and reticulations is difficult because automorphisms and symmetric/asymmetric configurations complicate direct enumeration. The paper aims to find a tractable counting scheme that avoids tracking component graphs and symmetry distinctions, and to extend exact counts beyond previously known cases.
AI.method: Define |P_{ℓ,k}| = W_k(ℓ) + D_k(ℓ), where W_k(ℓ) weights networks by inverse automorphism-group order and D_k(ℓ) is the remainder. Derive a recursion for W_k(ℓ) over source layers of the tree-component structure; show its exponential generating function is a Laurent polynomial in √(1−2x). For k≤5, interpret D_k(ℓ) as a weighted count of networks with a distinguished involution obeying an extended recursion, then symbolically evaluate both recursions.
AI.result: Automorphism groups of these networks are 2-groups, elementary abelian for k≤5 but not in general. Exact symbolic evaluation yields closed-form |P_{ℓ,k}| for k≤5, with k=5 new; it reproduces published counts for k≤4 and corrects a coefficient in a published generating function for k=3. Asymptotically, non-tree-child networks are a fraction 2k(k−1)/ℓ of tree-child networks to leading order, giving the third term of the asymptotic expansion of |P_{ℓ,k}|. Reticulation-visible networks exceed tree-child networks by fraction k(k−1)/ℓ, and a uniformly random network in P_{ℓ,k} has a nontrivial automorphism with probability k(k−1)/(4ℓ^3) to leading order.
AI.conclusion: The weighted-count-plus-defect framework provides an effective route to exact and asymptotic enumeration of phylogenetic networks, avoiding component lists and symmetry casework, extending closed forms to k=5, correcting earlier data, and yielding precise leading-order fractions for structural and symmetry-related classes.

title: Learning Latent Protein Languages for Autoregressive Generation
summary: Autoregressive transformers remain comparatively weak for protein sequence and structure generation. We study the role of target representation: amino acid tokens encode residue identities without explicit contextual semantics, while backbone coordinates require a discrete representation in our framework. We introduce two learned latent protein languages. Protein Latent Language (PLL) maps sequences to a 4,096-state contextual alphabet built on a frozen ESM-2 encoder, with one token per residue. Structure Latent Language (SLL) adapts GCP-VQVAE Lite with auxiliary sequence and confidence supervision while retaining decoding to backbone coordinates. We separately pretrain autoregressive transformer models on PLL and SLL tokens using next-token prediction, yielding PLLM and SLLM. Under matched downstream sequence training, PLLM has a fitted compute-scaling exponent of 0.038 versus 0.020 for the amino acid autoregressive model. In unconditional sequence generation, PLLM reduces the fraction of samples below a heuristic 1.5-bit residue-composition entropy threshold by 54% relative to the amino acid model across sampling temperatures. For sequence-to-structure prediction, replacing the original GCP-VQVAE Lite tokenizer with SLL reduces best validation perplexity by 34% under matched training. For long proteins, latent-token sampling is approximately 1,000 times faster than MSA-based AlphaFold2 in our measurements. In backbone generation, SLLM compares favorably with other generative models on diversity and novelty. We also observe early signs that using SLLM's internal token confidence for inference-time sampling can improve sequence-to-structure prediction quality beyond a single decoded sample. These results position learned latent protein languages as a promising substrate for autoregressive transformer scaling and inference-time sampling in protein generation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces two learned latent protein languages (PLL for sequences, SLL for structures) to improve autoregressive transformer generation of proteins, showing better scaling, quality, and speed.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive transformers remain comparatively weak for protein sequence and structure generation. The authors hypothesize that the target representation matters: amino acid tokens carry no explicit contextual semantics, and backbone coordinates require a discrete representation.
AI.method: They build Protein Latent Language (PLL), mapping sequences to a 4,096-state contextual alphabet via a frozen ESM-2 encoder (one token per residue), and Structure Latent Language (SLL), adapting GCP-VQVAE Lite with auxiliary sequence and confidence supervision while retaining backbone decoding. They pretrain autoregressive transformers on PLL and SLL tokens via next-token prediction to yield PLLM and SLLM.
AI.result: PLLM shows a higher compute-scaling exponent (0.038 vs 0.020) than the amino acid model and cuts low-entropy samples by 54%. SLL reduces best validation perplexity by 34% vs the original tokenizer. Latent-token sampling is ~1,000x faster than MSA-based AlphaFold2 for long proteins. SLLM is competitive on diversity and novelty, and internal token confidence can improve sequence-to-structure prediction.
AI.conclusion: Learned latent protein languages are a promising substrate for autoregressive transformer scaling and inference-time sampling in protein generation.

title: On the sensitivity to hyperparameters of a Bayesian method to infer selection signatures
summary: Motivated by a real-life problem, namely, inferring genomic regions affected by selection, we studied some properties of a two-step method that performs this task based on the FST. This approach exhibits computational simplicity as an appealing feature. Step one involves fitting a conjugate Bayesian model to find point estimates of FST and selecting the markers to be considered in step two, where they are grouped using such estimates. Subjective priors are frequently used in this problem and large hyperparameters may be encountered; hence, there is interest in addressing their impact. Preliminary analyses suggested that, the number of markers selected in step one tends to zero when the hyperparameters have the same value and tend to infinity, or are different but tend to infinity and their difference tends to zero. Thus, we studied how hyperparameters affect the posterior mean, variance, and predictive density of allele frequencies, and the posterior distribution of FST, formally. Moreover, an empirical approach based on simulated and real data was performed. Our main findings are summarized in two theorems that set the asymptotic behavior of the method, providing a foundation to understand the aforementioned phenomena. As to the empirical studies, the groups created in the second step, the estimated posterior means and the number of selected markers showed high sensitivity to hyperparameters. Albeit the mathematical intractability of the posterior distribution of FST, our results revealed asymptotic properties explaining two features of the method that lacked a formal elucidation.

AI.tldr: The paper formally studies how hyperparameters affect a two-step FST-based method for detecting genomic regions under selection, providing two asymptotic theorems and empirical validations of the method's sensitivity to hyperparameters.
AI.motivation: Motivated by inferring genomic regions affected by selection, the authors investigate a computationally simple two-step FST method. Subjective priors with large hyperparameters are common, and preliminary analyses suggested that the number of markers selected in step one tends to zero under certain hyperparameter conditions, motivating a formal study of hyperparameter impact.
AI.method: The method fits a conjugate Bayesian model to obtain point estimates of FST (step one) and selects markers, which are then grouped using those estimates (step two). The authors formally study how hyperparameters affect the posterior mean, variance, and predictive density of allele frequencies and the posterior distribution of FST, supported by simulated and real data experiments.
AI.result: Two theorems establish the asymptotic behavior of the method. Empirically, the groups created in step two, the estimated posterior means, and the number of selected markers showed high sensitivity to hyperparameters. The findings explain two features of the method that previously lacked formal elucidation despite the mathematical intractability of the FST posterior distribution.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a formal foundation for understanding hyperparameter effects in the two-step FST method, explaining observed asymptotic phenomena and highlighting the method's sensitivity to hyperparameter choices.

title: On the Spread of a Virus and Traveling Waves, Part I
summary: This paper develops a one-dimensional model for a mobile viral component propagating through a spatially distributed susceptible population. Random viral motion produces diffusion, whereas a response to the relative gradient of susceptible density generates directed transport. The existence of a positive entire traveling wave is proved when directed transport dominates diffusion, and the limiting case of equal transport and diffusion coefficients is constructed separately. A dimensionless transformation then converts the remaining equation into a logistic equation and supplies closed-form profiles. These formulas identify the unique viral maximum and the far-field behavior. A conservative implicit-explicit finite-difference method provides an independent numerical check. Diffusion is evaluated at the new time level, the gradient-driven flux explicitly at cell interfaces, and susceptible depletion pointwise. Exact traveling-wave values specify the initial data and time-dependent Dirichlet conditions at both endpoints. Thus, the computation tests preservation and translation of the analytical profiles. A calculation with eight hundred spatial subintervals reproduces the localized viral band and the monotone susceptible front. The largest uniform errors are approximately $1.70\cdot10^{-2}$ for viral density and $2.22\cdot10^{-3}$ for susceptible density. The numerical results corroborate the analytical construction and show that the conservative discretization captures the proposed propagation mechanism.

AI.tldr: A 1D model of a mobile viral component spreading through a spatially distributed susceptible population is developed, with diffusion from random motion and directed transport from the susceptible density gradient; traveling-wave solutions are proved and verified numerically.
AI.motivation: To describe how a mobile viral component propagates through a spatially distributed susceptible population, where random viral motion causes diffusion and a response to the relative gradient of susceptible density drives directed transport.
AI.method: A one-dimensional advection-diffusion-type model with diffusion plus gradient-driven directed transport. Existence of a positive entire traveling wave is proved when directed transport dominates diffusion, with the equal-coefficient limiting case constructed separately. A dimensionless transformation reduces the equation to a logistic equation yielding closed-form profiles. A conservative implicit-explicit finite-difference scheme is used: diffusion implicit, gradient-driven flux explicit at cell interfaces, susceptible depletion pointwise, with exact traveling-wave data as initial and Dirichlet boundary conditions.
AI.result: Closed-form traveling-wave profiles identify the unique viral maximum and far-field behavior. A computation with 800 spatial subintervals reproduces the localized viral band and monotone susceptible front, with largest uniform errors ~1.70e-2 for viral density and ~2.22e-3 for susceptible density.
AI.conclusion: The numerical results corroborate the analytical construction and show that the conservative discretization captures the proposed propagation mechanism of the viral band.

title: Reproducibility and Leakage-Controlled Evaluation of Machine-Learning Models for Chronic Kidney Disease Classification
summary: Near-perfect classification of small clinical datasets can hinge on preprocessing, data leakage, missing-data handling, and the evaluation sample. We reproduced a published chronic kidney disease (CKD) classification study on the UCI CKD dataset (400 records, 24 predictors) under explicit leakage controls. A stratified 70:30 development-holdout partition was fixed before any learned preprocessing; imputation, encoding, scaling, supervised feature selection, and PCA were fitted only within training folds. Nine classifiers, three feature representations, and three missing-data strategies were compared by 5x3 repeated stratified cross-validation and ranked on training cross-validation only (ties reported); a frozen set of finalists was evaluated once on the holdout (discrimination, calibration, Brier score), treated as a locked historical internal sample. Ablation, grouped SHAP values, three further seeds, and post hoc sensitivity analyses examined robustness. The top-ranked selected-feature pipeline (KNN imputation, Extra Trees) reached a repeated cross-validation accuracy of 0.9869 and a holdout accuracy of 0.9833 (exact 95% interval 0.9411-0.9980). PCA (27 components, 95.96% of variance) gave only a marginal, seed-dependent advantage over interpretable original-feature representations, and several pipelines were statistically indistinguishable. Nested resampling of the selection procedure gave an outer accuracy of 0.9845, 0.0095 below the top-ranked pipeline on the same folds; missingness indicators alone yielded a ROC area of 0.85-0.88, and removing renal, urinary, and hematologic fields cut accuracy to 0.89. High internal performance persisted after leakage controls but appears driven largely by clinically proximal laboratory and urinalysis variables and CKD-associated missingness; it is not clinical validation, and external, prospective evaluation remains necessary.

AI.tldr: Reproducing a published CKD classification study under strict leakage controls yields high internal accuracy (~0.98), but the performance is largely driven by clinically proximal lab/urinalysis variables and CKD-associated missingness, not clinical validation.
AI.motivation: Near-perfect classification on small clinical datasets can be an artifact of preprocessing, data leakage, missing-data handling, and evaluation sample choice. The authors aim to test whether a reported CKD classification result holds under explicit leakage controls and to assess what actually drives the high performance.
AI.method: Reproduced a published CKD study on the UCI CKD dataset (400 records, 24 predictors). Fixed a stratified 70:30 development-holdout split before any learned preprocessing; fitted imputation, encoding, scaling, feature selection, and PCA only within training folds. Compared 9 classifiers, 3 feature representations, and 3 missing-data strategies via 5x3 repeated stratified CV, ranked on CV only, and evaluated frozen finalists once on holdout (discrimination, calibration, Brier). Ran ablation, grouped SHAP, three additional seeds, and sensitivity analyses.
AI.result: Top pipeline (KNN imputation, Extra Trees, selected features) reached 0.9869 repeated CV accuracy and 0.9833 holdout accuracy (95% CI 0.9411-0.9980). PCA (27 components, 95.96% variance) gave only a marginal, seed-dependent advantage; several pipelines were statistically indistinguishable. Nested resampling gave outer accuracy 0.9845 (0.0095 below the top pipeline). Missingness indicators alone achieved ROC AUC 0.85-0.88; removing renal, urinary, and hematologic fields cut accuracy to 0.89.
AI.conclusion: High internal performance persists after leakage controls, but is driven largely by clinically proximal laboratory and urinalysis variables and CKD-associated missingness. This is not clinical validation; external, prospective evaluation remains necessary.

title: TempoBridge: Source-Conditioned Flow Matching with Optimal Transport Couplings for Single-Cell Population Transitions
summary: Destructive single-cell measurements provide unpaired population snapshots rather than observations of the same cells across conditions. Local cell states and transition requests may also be insufficient to distinguish responses across source populations. We introduce TempoBridge, a common source-conditioned transport formulation for temporal, genetic, and chemical population transitions. Source cells initialize latent transport and provide a fixed empirical population summary. The velocity field receives this summary alongside the evolving cell state, flow time, and a structured transition descriptor. Minibatch optimal transport (OT) supplies couplings only for conditional flow-matching training paths; inference requires neither target expression nor OT computation. On held-out donors, TempoBridge achieves an Energy distance of 0.129 versus 0.144 for scGen. Genetic mean-expression $L_2$ error is 2.261 versus 3.156 for scGPT-scratch under Seen 2/2. On held-out compounds, condition-averaged drug-effect correlation is 0.598 versus 0.561 for the CellFlow adapter. Temporal ablations show higher mean distributional error after removing source context, replacing optimal transport with random pairing, or replacing flow matching with static residual regression. Together, these results demonstrate the predictive utility of a common source-conditioned transport formulation across held-out donors, gene combinations, and compounds.

AI.tldr: TempoBridge is a common source-conditioned transport framework for modeling population transitions across temporal, genetic, and chemical perturbations, using minibatch OT only for training and requiring no target or OT at inference.
AI.motivation: Destructive single-cell measurements yield unpaired population snapshots, so local cell states and transition requests alone cannot distinguish responses across different source populations. A unified formulation conditioned on the source population is needed.
AI.method: TempoBridge uses a source-conditioned transport formulation where source cells initialize latent transport and provide a fixed empirical population summary. A velocity field takes the summary, evolving cell state, flow time, and a structured transition descriptor. Minibatch OT provides couplings only for conditional flow-matching training paths; inference needs neither target expression nor OT computation.
AI.result: Held-out donors: Energy distance 0.129 vs 0.144 (scGen). Genetic mean-expression L2 error 2.261 vs 3.156 (scGPT-scratch, Seen 2/2). Held-out compounds: drug-effect correlation 0.598 vs 0.561 (CellFlow adapter). Temporal ablations show higher distributional error without source context, with random pairing instead of OT, or with static residual regression instead of flow matching.
AI.conclusion: A common source-conditioned transport formulation provides predictive utility across held-out donors, gene combinations, and compounds.

title: Lightweight Semantic EEG Foundation Model for Frozen Cross-Disorder Transfer
summary: Large-scale EEG foundation models have demonstrated promising transferability across neurological disorders, but often require millions of parameters and substantial computational resources. In this paper, we present the Universal Semantic EEG Foundation Model (USE-FM), a lightweight EEG foundation model that learns transferable neural representations through self-supervised signal reconstruction on the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus (TUEG). After pretraining, the encoder is frozen and evaluated on two clinically distinct downstream tasks, abnormal EEG detection (TUAB) and epileptic seizure recognition (TUEP), using a unified frozen-transfer protocol against recent EEG foundation models, including LUNA-Base and CBraMod. With only 1.46 million parameters, approximately one-fifth the size of existing models, USE-FM achieves competitive overall performance, including strong sensitivity and F1-score on TUEP (SEN $75.00 \pm 14.14$, F1 $70.37 \pm 4.01$), while maintaining competitive performance on TUAB (AUC $85.24 \pm 5.61$). Beyond downstream classification, latent representation analysis using $k$-means clustering together with PCA and t-SNE demonstrates that USE-FM learns organized semantic EEG representations comparable to substantially larger foundation models. These results suggest that large-scale self-supervised pretraining enables lightweight architectures to learn transferable semantic EEG representations, providing a computationally efficient foundation for cross-disorder analysis and future clinical decision support in neurological disorders.

AI.tldr: USE-FM is a lightweight EEG foundation model (1.46M params) pretrained via self-supervised reconstruction on TUEG, achieving competitive frozen-transfer performance on TUAB and TUEP tasks and learning organized semantic representations.
AI.motivation: Large-scale EEG foundation models offer transferability across neurological disorders but demand millions of parameters and heavy computation, limiting accessibility. The paper aims to show that self-supervised pretraining can enable lightweight architectures to learn transferable semantic EEG representations efficiently.
AI.method: USE-FM is pretrained with self-supervised signal reconstruction on the TUEG corpus. After pretraining, the encoder is frozen and evaluated via a unified frozen-transfer protocol on two downstream tasks: abnormal EEG detection (TUAB) and epileptic seizure recognition (TUEP). Latent representations are analyzed using k-means clustering with PCA and t-SNE, and compared against recent EEG foundation models (LUNA-Base, CBraMod).
AI.result: With only 1.46M parameters (~one-fifth of existing models), USE-FM achieves competitive performance: TUEP sensitivity 75.00 ± 14.14 and F1 70.37 ± 4.01; TUAB AUC 85.24 ± 5.61. Representation analysis shows organized semantic EEG representations comparable to much larger models.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale self-supervised pretraining enables lightweight architectures to learn transferable semantic EEG representations, providing a computationally efficient foundation for cross-disorder analysis and future clinical decision support.

title: LifeLong Digital Twin: A Unified Modeling Paradigm and Agent Harness for Event-Driven Lifelong Health State Trajectories
summary: Human health is a continuous, dynamic trajectory shaped by the cumulative interplay of biological processes, clinical events, behaviors and environmental exposures across the life course. Unifying the full breadth of lifelong health information, including longitudinal records, genetic variation, molecular profiles and environmental histories, is essential for whole-person modeling and remains a major challenge. We introduce LifeLong Digital Twin, a unified, event-driven modeling paradigm that organizes Life Events into daily Health States and accumulates them into Lifelong Health Context. An accompanying Agent Harness incorporates multimodal evidence beyond the language model's textual context. We evaluate four language models across 25 disease endpoints on three tasks: Disease Trajectory Forecasting, Disease Risk Ranking and Multi-horizon Disease Prediction. The approach yields marked gains over the reference condition: model-averaged F1 increases by 22.0% for disease identification in trajectory forecasting and 18.3% for five-year disease outcomes; thyroid-disease F1 reaches 0.669. The framework provides a foundation for whole-person digital twins and research on personalized lifelong disease prevention.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces LifeLong Digital Twin, an event-driven paradigm that organizes lifelong Life Events into daily Health States and accumulates them into a Lifelong Health Context, with an Agent Harness incorporating multimodal evidence beyond text. It is evaluated on 25 disease endpoints across three tasks using four language models.
AI.motivation: Human health is a continuous, dynamic trajectory shaped by cumulative biological, clinical, behavioral, and environmental factors. Unifying full lifelong health information—longitudinal records, genetic variation, molecular profiles, and environmental histories—is essential for whole-person modeling but remains a major challenge.
AI.method: LifeLong Digital Twin is a unified, event-driven modeling paradigm that organizes Life Events into daily Health States and accumulates them into a Lifelong Health Context. An accompanying Agent Harness incorporates multimodal evidence beyond the language model's textual context.
AI.result: Four language models were evaluated across 25 disease endpoints on three tasks: Disease Trajectory Forecasting, Disease Risk Ranking, and Multi-horizon Disease Prediction. The approach yields marked gains over the reference condition: model-averaged F1 increases by 22.0% for disease identification in trajectory forecasting and 18.3% for five-year disease outcomes; thyroid-disease F1 reaches 0.669.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a foundation for whole-person digital twins and research on personalized lifelong disease prevention.

title: An evolutionary origin of collective decision making in humans and machines
comment: 39 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary materials (Materials and Methods, Supplementary Text, 12 supplementary figures) are appended to the main text
summary: Groups of individuals can solve collective problems more accurately than any single member, by aggregating their opinions. Recent theoretical work has identified individual-level reward schemes that allow uninformed individuals to evolve collective intelligence from the bottom up, through social learning. Yet these results are restricted to linear prediction problems and simple averaging, while the decision tasks that real groups confront are often non-linear, and the institutions that aggregate opinions are seldom single-layer averages: districts elect representatives who in turn vote on policy, referees advise editors who decide on publication. Here we develop a framework for the evolution of collective intelligence in multi-layer voting populations, where individuals observe limited information and groups recursively aggregate their opinions by majority rule. We prove that single-layer voting cannot solve non-linear classification problems under any individual reward scheme. We then identify a "marginal feedback" payoff structure, which rewards individuals only when their opinion is pivotal in their group, and at every layer above them. This reward scheme induces a layered population to evolve accurate collective solutions to complex, non-linear decision tasks through individual-level peer imitation alone. The collective behavior that emerges is equivalent to a multi-layer perceptron in machine learning. Our results provide a naturalistic account of hierarchical institutions, in which the outsize importance of swing voters is the incentive that sustains collective accuracy; and they identify the credit-assignment rule in machine learning as not just an engineered solution but a natural evolutionary outcome.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a framework showing that multi-layer voting populations can evolve collective intelligence for non-linear tasks via a "marginal feedback" reward scheme, equivalent to a multi-layer perceptron.
AI.motivation: Prior theoretical work on the evolution of collective intelligence is limited to linear prediction and simple averaging, whereas real decision tasks are non-linear and aggregation institutions are hierarchical (e.g., districts elect representatives, referees advise editors).
AI.method: The authors model multi-layer voting populations where individuals have limited information and groups recursively aggregate opinions by majority rule. They prove single-layer voting cannot solve non-linear classification under any reward scheme, then introduce a "marginal feedback" payoff that rewards individuals only when their opinion is pivotal in their group and at every layer above.
AI.result: Single-layer voting fails on non-linear classification under any individual reward scheme. The marginal feedback scheme enables a layered population to evolve accurate collective solutions to complex non-linear tasks through peer imitation alone, with emergent behavior equivalent to a multi-layer perceptron.
AI.conclusion: The results offer a naturalistic account of hierarchical institutions where swing voters' importance sustains collective accuracy, and identify the credit-assignment rule in machine learning as a natural evolutionary outcome rather than an engineered solution.

title: Multi-type branching diffusions with small mutation rates
summary: Approximate solutions are found for Feller-like neutral multi-type branching diffusions $\big{(}\mathbf{X}(t)\big{)}_{t \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}}$ in the limit of small mutation rates. The method employed involves solving approximations to the Laplace transformed forward Kolmogorov equation by integrating along characteristics. To leading order in the scale $θ$ of the overall mutation rate the super-critical diffusion is found to collapse onto a line density aligned with the stationary left eigenvector of the rate matrix following a rapid change of behaviour at a critical time $t_{\rm c}$, which has a weak logarithmic dependence on $θ$. First order in $θ$ approximations to the density and moments of $\mathbf{X}(t)$ are also determined. The first-order approximation corresponds to allowing at most one mutation in the coalescent tree of a sample and is valid for $t < t_{\rm c}$ in the supercritical case, and more generally for the critical and sub-critical cases.

AI.tldr: The paper derives approximate solutions for Feller-like neutral multi-type branching diffusions in the small mutation rate limit by solving the Laplace-transformed forward Kolmogorov equation along characteristics.
AI.motivation: Understanding how multi-type branching diffusions behave when mutation rates are small, particularly the dynamics of type frequencies and moment approximations.
AI.method: Solve approximations to the Laplace transformed forward Kolmogorov equation by integrating along characteristics, expanding to leading and first order in the mutation rate scale θ.
AI.result: To leading order the super-critical diffusion collapses onto a line density aligned with the stationary left eigenvector of the rate matrix, after a rapid behavioural change at a critical time t_c with weak logarithmic dependence on θ. First-order density and moment approximations are obtained, valid for t < t_c in the supercritical case and generally for critical/sub-critical cases.
AI.conclusion: The first-order approximation corresponds to allowing at most one mutation in the coalescent tree of a sample, providing tractable approximations for small mutation rates.

title: End-to-End Autonomous Recursive Arborescence Deformable Flow and Non-Linear Hemodynamics for Patient-Specific Coronary Centerline Extraction
summary: Extracting patient-specific vascular trees from volumetric medical images is fundamental to computational angiography and non-invasive hemodynamic assessment. Conventional voxel segmentation models often sever delicate bifurcations, while heuristic Euclidean Minimum Spanning Trees introduce non-anatomical shortcuts. Moreover, linear Poiseuille flow neglects quadratic kinetic dissipation across arterial narrowings, underestimating ischemia. We formulate an end-to-end framework decoupling continuous geometric arborescence generation from non-linear hemodynamics. First, an autonomous 3D Ostium Landmark Localization Head with dual-sinus query channels and spherical-gated refinement eliminates centerline seeding dependency, achieving cohort mean localization error of 7.63 mm (7.43 mm LCA, 7.83 mm RCA; 71.4% <= 8.0 mm) from raw contrast context. Second, a Spatially-Grounded Deformable Step Flow Architecture queries continuous 3D feature pyramids via trilinear sampling, sequentially generating trajectories with anchor boundary enforcement (X(0) = P_start). Third, a Top-Down Recursive Arborescence State Machine detects bifurcation peaks via Tree-NMS and parameterizes predecessor parent pointers (p_k < k), guaranteeing single connected acyclic tree topology (beta_0 = 1, beta_1 = 0) with differentiable step termination. Fourth, an iterative Picard non-linear Kirchhoff solver with Young-Tsai / Gould quadratic dissipation enforces machine-precision mass conservation (residual 5.82e-11 mL/s). Across 14 development patients under standardized in-silico stenosis stress testing (Q_0 = 4.0 mL/s), linear Poiseuille flow misclassifies 75% diameter lesions as non-ischemic (FFR > 0.80) in 14/14 cases, whereas our non-linear solver captures functional ischemia (FFR = 0.5864, lesion disparity 32.89 mmHg, p = 6.10e-5) with 3.66x collateral shunting. Test set firewall isolation was maintained.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end framework separates continuous 3D vascular tree generation from non-linear hemodynamics, improving bifurcation preservation and ischemia detection over voxel segmentation and linear Poiseuille models.
AI.motivation: Conventional voxel segmentation severs delicate bifurcations, Euclidean MST shortcuts create non-anatomical paths, and linear Poiseuille flow neglects quadratic kinetic dissipation, underestimating ischemia across arterial narrowings.
AI.method: Four components: (1) autonomous 3D Ostium Landmark Localization Head with dual-sinus query channels and spherical-gated refinement; (2) Spatially-Grounded Deformable Step Flow Architecture using trilinear sampling over feature pyramids with anchor boundary enforcement; (3) Top-Down Recursive Arborescence State Machine with Tree-NMS and parent pointers ensuring single connected acyclic topology; (4) iterative Picard non-linear Kirchhoff solver with Young-Tsai/Gould quadratic dissipation.
AI.result: Ostium localization error 7.63 mm (7.43 LCA, 7.83 RCA; 71.4% <= 8.0 mm). Machine-precision mass conservation (residual 5.82e-11 mL/s). In 14 patients, linear Poiseuille misclassifies 75% diameter lesions in 14/14 cases (FFR>0.80); non-linear solver captures ischemia (FFR=0.5864, disparity 32.89 mmHg, p=6.10e-5) with 3.66x collateral shunting.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling geometric arborescence generation from non-linear hemodynamics yields anatomically valid vascular trees and physiologically accurate ischemia assessment, outperforming linear flow assumptions.

title: CoHyFuse: Condition-wise Hypergraph Fusion with Global Connectome in Task-fMRI
comment: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM 2026)
summary: Task-fMRI connectomes reveal state-dependent neural reconfigurations, yet conventional methods marginalize these signals by aggregating distinct conditions into static pairwise graphs, thereby obscuring condition-specific multi-ROI organization. We introduce CoHyFuse, a condition-aware ROI-centered hypergraph framework that constructs a task-state-specific incidence matrix from condition-wise functional connectivity (FC)-profile embeddings, allowing the same ROI to form different multi-ROI hyperedges across task phases. Condition-specific neighborhood sizes $K_q$ further adapt the hyperedge scale to each task state, and the resulting condition embeddings are fused with a complementary whole-session FC branch for prediction. In the AABC cohort (N=1,074), CoHyFuse achieved the best mean out-of-fold predictive performance among evaluated baselines on FACENAME Fluid Cognition Composite (FCC) prediction (7.83$\pm$0.10 MAE, 0.439$\pm$0.026 \(R^2\)) and VISMOTOR age prediction (7.52$\pm$0.37 MAE, 0.592$\pm$0.022 \(R^2\)). In an auxiliary CMI-HBN attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) classification benchmark (N=223), CoHyFuse obtained 72.0$\pm$2.1\% macro-AUC and 74.2$\pm$2.9\% accuracy. Ablation studies support the contributions of condition-wise incidence construction and dual-view fusion, suggesting that state-resolved ROI-set structure provides complementary predictive information beyond whole-session FC alone. Occlusion analysis identifies the Distraction condition as the primary driver of model prediction, pointing toward the Salience/Ventral Attention Network (SAN)--FrontoParietal Network (FPN) and within-SAN hyperedge-defined ROI-set motifs as candidate model-relevant patterns. This framework provides an interpretable, state-resolved view of the connectome for downstream cohort analysis.

AI.tldr: CoHyFuse is a condition-aware ROI-centered hypergraph framework that preserves task-state-specific connectivity by building condition-wise incidence matrices, improving cognition/age prediction and ADHD classification over static FC baselines.
AI.motivation: Conventional task-fMRI connectome methods aggregate distinct task conditions into static pairwise graphs, marginalizing condition-specific signals and obscuring condition-specific multi-ROI organization.
AI.method: CoHyFuse constructs a task-state-specific incidence matrix from condition-wise FC-profile embeddings, letting the same ROI form different multi-ROI hyperedges across task phases. Condition-specific neighborhood sizes K_q adapt hyperedge scale per state. Resulting condition embeddings are fused with a complementary whole-session FC branch for prediction.
AI.result: AABC cohort (N=1,074): best mean out-of-fold performance for FACENAME FCC prediction (7.83±0.10 MAE, 0.439±0.026 R²) and VISMOTOR age prediction (7.52±0.37 MAE, 0.592±0.022 R²). CMI-HBN ADHD benchmark (N=223): 72.0±2.1% macro-AUC, 74.2±2.9% accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Ablations support contributions of condition-wise incidence construction and dual-view fusion; state-resolved ROI-set structure adds complementary information beyond whole-session FC. Occlusion analysis highlights the Distraction condition and SAN-FPN / within-SAN ROI-set motifs as model-relevant. The framework offers an interpretable, state-resolved view of the connectome.

title: Unraveling phenotypic variation in multiscale behavioral dynamics
comment: Main text: 11 pages, 6 figures; SI: 13 pages, 9 figures
summary: Behavioral variability reflects differences in internal and external parameters and provides a substrate for natural selection. However, uncovering its structure is challenging because behavior evolves nonlinearly across multiple timescales. Our goal is to reconstruct phenotypic variation from finite behavioral observations without prescribing the scales at which individuals should be compared. To achieve this, we introduce a multiscale dissimilarity that compares dynamics across all statistically resolvable resolutions by constructing reduced transfer operators at progressively finer scales and weighting their differences by finite-sampling uncertainty. This dissimilarity defines a geometry of dynamical phenotypes, which we reconstruct using diffusion maps. We show that the resulting phenotypic coordinates locally follow the parameter directions to which dynamics are most sensitive. We validate our approach in a stochastic model and apply it to bacterial and larval zebrafish behavior. In bacteria, we identify run speed as a major component of inter-individual variability, associated with the chemotaxis protein CheB. In zebrafish, we find that prior prey experience reshapes behavioral dynamics and phenotypic variability, with paramecia experience concentrating fish in a prey-capture-associated region of phenotypic space. Together, these results provide a framework for identifying internal and environmental variables that structure dynamical phenotypes across scales.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a multiscale dissimilarity based on reduced transfer operators weighted by finite-sampling uncertainty, defining a geometry of dynamical phenotypes reconstructed via diffusion maps, and applies it to uncover behavioral variability structure in bacteria and zebrafish.
AI.motivation: Behavioral variability reflects internal and external parameter differences and underlies natural selection, but its structure is hard to uncover because behavior evolves nonlinearly across multiple timescales. The goal is to reconstruct phenotypic variation from finite observations without prescribing comparison scales.
AI.method: A multiscale dissimilarity compares dynamics across all statistically resolvable resolutions by building reduced transfer operators at progressively finer scales and weighting their differences by finite-sampling uncertainty. This dissimilarity defines a geometry of dynamical phenotypes, reconstructed using diffusion maps.
AI.result: The resulting phenotypic coordinates locally follow the parameter directions to which dynamics are most sensitive. Validation in a stochastic model and applications to bacterial and larval zebrafish behavior: in bacteria, run speed is a major component of inter-individual variability linked to chemotaxis protein CheB; in zebrafish, prior prey experience reshapes behavioral dynamics and phenotypic variability, with paramecia experience concentrating fish in a prey-capture-associated region of phenotypic space.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a framework for identifying internal and environmental variables that structure dynamical phenotypes across scales.

title: Random Genetic Variation Links Personality to Earnings and Wealth
summary: Personality is associated with economic outcomes, but whether these relationships are causal remains unclear. We exploit within-family variation in genetic propensity toward the Big Five generated by random genetic transmission from parents to offspring. Combining polygenic indexes from the Lifelines cohort study with 19 years of administrative tax records in the Netherlands, we find that greater genetic propensity toward emotional stability increases earnings and household wealth, while genetic propensity toward conscientiousness increases household wealth. The other three traits show no consistent pattern across outcomes and specifications. The effect of genetic propensity toward emotional stability on earnings remains positive as we progressively account for genetic propensity toward educational attainment, cognitive performance, and depression. These findings strengthen the evidence that personality causally affects earnings and wealth.

AI.tldr: Using within-family genetic variation, the study finds that genetic propensity toward emotional stability raises earnings and household wealth, while conscientiousness raises household wealth, supporting a causal link between personality and economic outcomes.
AI.motivation: Personality is linked to economic outcomes, but it is unclear whether the relationship is causal or confounded by family background and other factors.
AI.method: Exploits within-family variation in genetic propensity toward the Big Five from random genetic transmission from parents to offspring, combining polygenic indexes from the Lifelines cohort with 19 years of Dutch administrative tax records.
AI.result: Greater genetic propensity toward emotional stability increases earnings and household wealth; conscientiousness increases household wealth. The other three traits show no consistent pattern. The emotional stability effect on earnings stays positive when accounting for genetic propensity toward educational attainment, cognitive performance, and depression.
AI.conclusion: The findings strengthen evidence that personality causally affects earnings and wealth.

title: Classification of strongly non-hyperbolic critical points of planar second-order chemical reaction systems
summary: The dynamics of chemical reaction systems with two chemical species can be described (under mass-action kinetics) by planar autonomous systems of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with right-hand sides containing polynomials. While their behaviour close to hyperbolic critical points is well understood, their dynamics has not been fully characterized for strongly non-hyperbolic critical points, where the linearization close to the equilibrium is given by the zero matrix. In this paper, the behaviour of such chemical reaction systems is investigated. Considering second-order chemical reaction networks with a positive equilibrium point, we show that only nine geometric equivalence classes are possible out of the sixteen classes for general ODE systems. Examples of chemical reaction networks in each class are presented. All sixteen geometric equivalence classes can be realized by chemical systems if the non-hyperbolic equilibrium point is located at the origin.

AI.tldr: This paper classifies strongly non-hyperbolic critical points (linearization = zero matrix) in planar mass-action chemical reaction networks with two species, showing only 9 of 16 geometric equivalence classes occur for positive equilibria, while all 16 are realizable at the origin.
AI.motivation: Reaction systems are modeled as planar polynomial ODEs, and their behavior near hyperbolic equilibria is well understood. However, strongly non-hyperbolic critical points remain uncharacterized in this chemical context.
AI.method: Study second-order reaction networks with two species and a positive equilibrium; analyze planar autonomous polynomial ODEs with zero linearization matrix, classifying orbit geometry into 16 possible equivalence classes and determining which arise chemically.
AI.result: For positive equilibria, only 9 of the 16 geometric equivalence classes are possible in chemical systems, with explicit example networks given for each. If the non-hyperbolic equilibrium is at the origin, all 16 classes can be realized.
AI.conclusion: Chemical constraints restrict strongly non-hyperbolic dynamics at positive equilibria to 9 classes, but no such restriction holds at the origin, where all 16 general classes appear.

title: Self-assembly Monte Carlo reveals localized entanglement in giant polymer melts
comment: Main text: 12 pages and 6 figures. Supplementary material: 11 pages and 12 figures
summary: Topological entanglements are central to understanding and predicting the properties of polymer melts. Yet, they make equilibrium sampling computationally challenging, as decorrelation times grow rapidly with chain length. Here, we introduce a Monte Carlo scheme that bypasses typical computational bottlenecks by working in a self-assembly ensemble rather than at fixed composition. Strictly local moves efficiently propagate backbone reconnections across scales while conserving the number of linear chains, achieving near-linear scaling of decorrelation time with system size, $τ_{\rm eq}\sim V^{1.0}$. With this method, formulated for a fully-packed lattice, we equilibrate periodic systems totalling up to $\simeq 1.1\times 10^9$ monomers, accessing a universal melt regime insensitive to lattice details. We analyze intra- and inter-chain entanglements for chains of up to $N\simeq 5 \times 10^5$ monomers, revealing that they manifest as localized knots and links rather than as global tangles. Finally, we show that the magnitude of the Gauss linking integral between neighbouring chains grows only as $N^{1/4}$.

AI.tldr: A Monte Carlo method in a self-assembly ensemble equilibrates fully-packed lattice polymer melts up to ~10^9 monomers, showing entanglements appear as localized knots/links and linking number scales as N^{1/4}.
AI.motivation: Topological entanglements govern polymer melt properties, but equilibrium sampling is hard because decorrelation times grow rapidly with chain length.
AI.method: Monte Carlo scheme working in a self-assembly ensemble instead of fixed composition; strictly local moves propagate backbone reconnections across scales while conserving the number of linear chains; formulated for a fully-packed lattice.
AI.result: Achieves near-linear scaling of decorrelation time with system size (τ_eq ~ V^1.0); equilibrates periodic systems up to ~1.1×10^9 monomers, accessing a universal melt regime insensitive to lattice details. Intra-/inter-chain entanglements analyzed for chains up to N ~ 5×10^5 monomers; entanglements manifest as localized knots and links rather than global tangles; Gauss linking integral between neighboring chains grows only as N^{1/4}.
AI.conclusion: The method enables large-scale equilibrium sampling of entangled polymer melts, revealing that topological entanglements are local in nature and that inter-chain linking magnitude grows slowly (N^{1/4}) with chain length.

title: NeuroCBIR: A Fast and Accurate Image Retrieval System for Whole-Brain and Region-Specific MRI
comment: Neuroimaging, Content-Based Image Retrieval, MRI, Zero-Shot Learning
summary:
Content-based image retrieval (CBIR) in neuroimaging enables the identification of structurally similar brain scans, supporting diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning; however, existing methods are often limited to small datasets, single brain regions, or coarse class labels, thereby restricting their clinical utility and generalizability.
  Here, we present NeuroCBIR, a framework for fast and flexible retrieval of both whole-brain and region-specific 3D T1w MRI scans. A total of 103 cortical and subcortical regions are extracted to enable both whole-brain and region-level queries.
  NeuroCBIR leverages latent representations learned by a variational autoencoder (VAE) combined with contrastive learning, producing scan-specific embeddings that capture anatomical patterns. These embeddings were evaluated for subject re-identification, zero-shot age prediction, and zero-shot multi-class pathology stratification. Re-identification performance was high across both whole-brain and brain-region levels (mean average precision across the top-5 retrieved images (mAP@5) >= 98.4%), with robust generalization across datasets and acquisition conditions. While NeuroCBIR is not trained for age prediction or pathology stratification, zero-shot evaluations for these two tasks demonstrate that the embeddings encode meaningful information for downstream tasks.
  Embedding extraction on a 4-core CPU required approximately 18.7 s per scan, whereas similarity search was effectively instantaneous (less than 0.01 s).
  NeuroCBIR is publicly available for brain MRI with more than 26,000 precomputed T1w MRI embeddings. It supports reproducible research, region-specific flexibility, and clinically meaningful personalized diagnostic support. The software is available at https://github.com/minnelab/NeuroCBIR.

AI.tldr: NeuroCBIR is a content-based image retrieval framework for whole-brain and region-specific 3D T1w MRI, using VAE + contrastive learning embeddings, achieving high re-identification and zero-shot downstream performance.
AI.motivation: Existing CBIR methods in neuroimaging are limited to small datasets, single brain regions, or coarse class labels, restricting clinical utility and generalizability.
AI.method: Extracts 103 cortical and subcortical regions; leverages VAE latent representations combined with contrastive learning to produce scan-specific embeddings capturing anatomical patterns; supports whole-brain and region-level queries; evaluated on subject re-identification, zero-shot age prediction, and zero-shot multi-class pathology stratification.
AI.result: Re-identification mAP@5 >= 98.4% across whole-brain and region levels with robust generalization. Embedding extraction ~18.7 s/scan on 4-core CPU; similarity search <0.01 s. Zero-shot evaluations show embeddings encode meaningful downstream information.
AI.conclusion: NeuroCBIR enables fast, flexible, region-specific retrieval, supporting reproducible research and clinically meaningful personalized diagnostic support; publicly available with 26,000+ precomputed embeddings at https://github.com/minnelab/NeuroCBIR.
